Executive Summary.Sales and Marketing: CARI Health ("CARI") is pre-revenue and plans to sell a quantitative point-of-care methadone and EDDP blood test, delivered as a placed reader plus a single-use cassette, to opioid treatment programs (OTPs), which the Company sizes at about 2,300 programs treating an estimated 750,000 patients in 2025 and roughly 1.1 million patients by 2032. The market is concentrated, with ten operators running 836 clinics and about 300,100 patients, so the plan relies on five direct sales representatives at launch for the largest operators and a distribution partner for the remaining independent programs. Customer interest is documented by 13 signed letters: 3 letters of intent (Acadia, Crossroads and, on October 27, 2026, distributor MedSTAT Supplies), 1 memorandum of understanding with Community Medical Services and 9 letters of support. Twelve come from organizations treating more than 100,000 patients across 39 states; MedSTAT states that it supplies about 1,600 OTPs. None of these letters is a purchase commitment or a distribution agreement, as expected at this stage (before design freeze there is no final product or price to commit to, and FDA policy does not permit orders for a device awaiting 510(k) clearance): the Community Medical Services memorandum covers clinic space and patient referrals for the pilot study, the Johns Hopkins letter is less committal than the others, and the Acadia letter states a non-binding intent to deploy research-use-only units and to purchase after clearance. The business model sells readers at cost ($1,750) and earns on cassettes priced at $60, with 5.4 tests per patient per year, which produces about $288 of net revenue per patient per year at the 2032 channel mix after distributor margin. Payment depends on clinics billing Medicare add-on code G2077, which paid $151.93 in 2026 for a periodic dosing assessment, because no CARI-specific code exists and the reimbursement advisor found no payer coverage policy for quantitative methadone monitoring; the $60 price is about 40% of that rate, and Medicaid rates generally run lower. Market research supports the need, as a Research Collective provider survey described current practice as "dosing in the dark" and a 2026 JAMA Network Open study cited by the Company found that about 73% of patients at the median program leave treatment within six months. The Company's figures of about $400,000 of annual revenue lost to dropout per clinic and a $100,000 annual clinic gain from a 10% retention improvement rest on management's own analysis, and no evidence yet shows that CARI testing improves retention, which the board has identified as the outcome that must be proven. The forecast moves from $18,000 of research-use-only revenue in 2027 to $1.9 million in 2028 and $83.6 million in 2032, which requires about 950 patient enrollments per business day in 2032, with more than half of 2032 revenue coming from growth over 2031 and the $60 test price the model's largest single sensitivity. The October 25, 2026 model adds downside cases: at a 15% share of national patients 2032 revenue is $48.3 million, at 10% it is $32.2 million, and at 10% with a 12-month clearance delay it is $14.5 million; Scenario 5 of the November 2, 2026 model, a 12-month clearance delay at base penetration, gives 2032 revenue of $37.7 million and EBITDA of $15.8 million, with about $0.3 million of additional capital needed. Discrepancies identified during diligence arose largely from materials prepared at different stages of the product pivot. The Due Diligence Team regards the commercial case as credible but unproven until clearance, pilot data and a first paying customer are in hand. This profile is typical of a pre-clearance diagnostic: the Seed 2 round funds the pilot, design freeze and preparation for the second Pre-Submission, while the clinical validation study and 510(k) depend on the Series A.
Executive Summary.Financial: CARI has no product revenue. Reported revenue consists entirely of NIH grant funding recognized as allowable costs are incurred: $427,058 in FY2024 and $814,369 in FY2025, with net losses of $609,855 and $139,371. In January–June 2026, grant funding of $524,417 covered substantially all operating expenses of $499,242, with only $6,165 of costs not eligible for grant reimbursement. At June 30, 2026, the balance sheet showed cash of $195,061, total assets of $334,827, total liabilities of $192,832 (mainly $205,000 of convertible notes) and equity of $141,995, and the August 31, 2026 bank statements show combined balances of about $256,500. CARI has raised $10.1 million in total, of which $7.0 million funded the discontinued wearable monitor program, so the current point-of-care platform has been funded by $2.84 million of BluePrint MedTech grants and $280,000 of Seed 2 notes. The open Seed 2 round is a $1.0 million convertible note with a $9.0 million pre-money cap, a 20% discount, 6% interest and 25% warrant coverage on the first $750,000, of which $280,000 is funded, $120,000 is soft circled (not a written commitment) and $600,000 remains. The $150,000 of contingent participation by Cove Fund and Charles Patton is excluded because the $400,000 threshold in the Cove side letter has not been met; on October 21, 2026 Cove confirmed by email that it will invest its $100,000 once that threshold is reached. Management projects EBITDA-positive operations in 2030 on revenue of $17.9 million, rising to $83.6 million and an 85% gross margin in 2032, but the projections assume moderate-complexity 510(k) clearance in 2028 and a CLIA waiver in 2028–2029. The October 25 model shows that a 10% share with a 12-month clearance delay would need up to about $11.9 million of additional capital, while Scenario 5 of the November 2, 2026 model (a 12-month delay at base penetration, costs and hiring held at plan) shows 2032 revenue of $37.7 million, positive EBITDA in 2031 and about $0.3 million of additional capital needed, an upper bound before any re-timing of the commercial build; denial is not modeled. Liquidity is thin, as year-end 2025 cash was $205,937, the model's cash low is about $200,000 in July 2027 ahead of a Series A targeted to close in August 2027, and the Company's 13-month forecast shows funds running out in August 2027 at the current budget if no further notes are sold (or January 2028 at a reduced $70,000 monthly run rate, assuming an NIH no-cost extension), and the board lists funding the clinical validation study as its highest-rated risk. Total capital to profitability is stated as $20 million, comprising the $2.5 million Phase II grant, the $1.0 million Seed 2 note, a $10 million Series A at an assumed $45 million pre-money valuation and a $6.5 million Series B, and the Series A and Series B valuations are management estimates rather than negotiated terms. The $543 million illustrative 2032 exit value applies a 6.5 times revenue multiple and, in the Due Diligence Team's view, should carry limited weight before clearance. The Company's runway reflects cash of about $256,500 plus about $1.0 million of awarded NIH grant funding that reimburses research costs through June 2027, consistent with the runway described in the January 2026 board minutes, and the March 2027 decisions on two pending grant applications ($9.5 million and about $8.65 million) remain open.
Executive Summary.Team: CARI is led by founder and CEO Patrik Schmidle, who has been part of seven company exits: four acquisitions as an executive (2000 to 2022) and three earlier-career transactions in which he was a shareholder and option holder without an active role (the Company has supplied a public source for each, which the Team has not independently verified) and who serves under a 2022 executive employment agreement providing a 50% target bonus and $200,000 of severance on termination without cause. The copy of that agreement in the data room states no base salary amount and contains no confidentiality or invention-assignment covenant of its own. Mr. Schmidle is a named inventor only on the 63/806,333 family, which he has assigned to the Company, so all patent filings are assigned to CARI; on November 6, 2026 he also signed a Confidential Information Non-Disclosure and Inventions Assignment Agreement (CIIAA) and a mutual arbitration agreement, whose forms the board approved for all current and future employees by unanimous written consent of all three directors on November 5–6, 2026. The CIIAA presently assigns his inventions to the Company, extends to work performed before signing and lists no prior inventions, so confidentiality and invention assignment now also cover know-how and earlier work; the amendment of his employment agreement (base salary, severance terms and a non-solicitation covenant) remains open. The Company's Team Compensation History shows the salaries actually paid since 2021 and states that no salary is deferred or accrued. Signed offer letters for Mr. McFarland ($225,000; October 8, 2025), Mr. Chon ($125,000; May 1, 2026) and Ms. Russell ($66,600; January 2024), and Ms. Russell's 2023 salary adjustment to $100,000, are now in the data room and agree with the Team Compensation History. The CEO states that he has deliberately kept his salary low to extend the runway and fund critical technical hires, and that the $200,000 salary in the financial model is the salary expected after the Series A closes. The Company has four full-time employees plus specialist consultants: Judson McFarland (VP Product Development, with over 25 years in diagnostics at Quidel, Abbott, Prometheus, ProciseDx and Biosynex), Kevin Chon (Senior Scientist, employed since May 2026; his signed offer letter states a June 1, 2026 start date) and Laurie Russell (Operations Director, employed since 2021). The technical and regulatory bench is drawn largely from ProciseDx, including Subha Selvaraju, whose biography credits her with a team that achieved FDA De Novo clearance of therapeutic drug monitoring assays, and regulatory consultant Eric Koehler, whose stated 100-plus FDA clearances and approvals span 510(k), De Novo, PMA and IDE submissions. Much of that expertise is engaged as hourly consultants under agreements with rates from $60 to $275 per hour that include invention assignment, which gives flexibility but limited retention protection. Torsten Fiebig served as Chief Science Officer from June 2020 and as a consultant from December 2023 until the 2024 pivot; the role has been vacant since, the board paused CSO and CTO recruiting in January 2026 for funding reasons, and a CSO is planned after the Series A, Foster Carr moved from Chief Medical Officer to medical consultant, and two separation agreements were signed in September 2024 when the wearable electrochemistry team was replaced with a diagnostics team drawn largely from ProciseDx and Prometheus. The board consists of Gioia Messinger, Charles Patton and the CEO, with Keith Richter and Damoder Reddy attending as observers and Cove Fund holding a conditional right to designate a director. Several advisors and board participants also hold Seed 2 notes, including Keith Richter ($50,000), Edward Kopetsky ($50,000), Suraj Achar ($50,000) and Eric Koehler ($30,000), investments made by people with the closest view of the Company on the same terms as other investors, which the Due Diligence Team treats both as a signal of conviction and as a financial interest when weighing the independence of their input. The advisory board includes Carla Marienfeld of UC San Diego, Kenneth Stoller of the Johns Hopkins Broadway Center and Brenda Davis, while Robert Sherrick of Community Medical Services left in December 2025 to avoid the appearance of a conflict and the Company has disclosed that the Sunrise clinician who wrote a letter of support is a grant co-investigator. The Due Diligence Team views the team as strong in diagnostics development and FDA experience but thinly staffed, with four employees and a vacant CSO role. Retention option grants are in place for Mr. McFarland (157,000; his October 8, 2025 offer letter specified 152,000, a difference the Company should explain) and Mr. Chon (50,000), the CEO reports reference checks on Mr. McFarland with five former colleagues, and no background check results are in the data room. The investigator approved by the IRB for the CMS pilot is Dr. Sherrick, the CMS Chief Science Officer who left the advisory board in December 2025.
Executive Summary.Intellectual Property: CARI's portfolio consists of four pending filings and no issued patents: US provisional 63/806,333 on point-of-care methadone and EDDP quantification (filed May 15, 2025), PCT/US2026/028473 claiming its priority (filed May 15, 2026), US provisional 64/067,115 on segregation of detection elements in multiplex assays (filed May 15, 2026) and US provisional 64/122,780 on whole blood processing for hematocrit-corrected measurement (filed July 30, 2026). The two newer provisionals must be converted within twelve months of their filing dates, which falls on May 15, 2027 and July 30, 2027, and management plans to convert both by mid-2027. Chain of title is documented for the first families, as all nine named inventors on the PCT application, including four Abingdon Health personnel, signed assignments to CARI, and the PCT assignment was recorded at the USPTO on August 18, 2026. The Abingdon consulting agreement of October 9, 2024, added to the data room after the diligence review noted its absence, assigns inventions to CARI including work performed before signing and pre-dates both the May 2025 provisional and the July 2025 assignments. Executed assignments of provisional 64/067,115 (signed by Judson McFarland and Kevin Chon on May 28, 2026; recorded June 5, 2026, Reel/Frame 74872/0405) and provisional 64/122,780 (signed by Judson McFarland, Kevin Chon, Chris Johnson and Corey Dambacher on October 12, 2026; recorded October 24, 2026, Reel/Frame 76493/0982) are now in the data room. Patent counsel (Procopio) completed a patent landscape review and found no active, relevant patent documents. Executive Summary.Corporate Documents: CARI Health, Inc. is a Delaware corporation incorporated on September 17, 2021. A certified copy from the Delaware Secretary of State (October 26, 2026) shows every charter document on file: the Certificate of Incorporation and Certificate of Conversion (September 17, 2021) and restated certificates filed July 9, 2024, November 19, 2024 and August 15, 2025, and a certificate of good standing of the same date confirms annual reports filed and franchise taxes paid. Executive Summary.Contracts: CARI has no signed customer purchase contracts, as expected at this stage: before design freeze there is no final product or price to commit to, FDA policy does not permit orders for a device awaiting 510(k) clearance, and purchase commitments are a post-clearance milestone. Its signed intent from operators treating about 101,500 patients, the MedSTAT distribution letter of intent (about 1,600 OTPs), the pilot-study MOU and planned 2027 research-use-only placements represent strong early commercial engagement for a pre-clearance diagnostic. Its commercial paper consists of a non-binding Acadia letter of intent dated August 8, 2025, a non-binding Crossroads letter of intent dated April 26, 2026, a non-binding distribution letter of intent from MedSTAT Supplies dated October 27, 2026 (estimating an 18% to 20% distribution margin), nine letters of support and a research-only memorandum with Community Medical Services dated August 17, 2026. Government funding is documented by notices of award, including NIH/NIDA BluePrint MedTech award U44 DA059627 (Year 1 $318,172, Year 2 $1,447,789 and Year 3 $1,069,475, the last issued June 19, 2026), which is paid on a cost-reimbursement basis, with about $1.97 million of backlog at year-end 2025 expected to be drawn through June 2027. Two UG3/UH3 applications for $9.5 million and about $8.65 million are pending, with scientific review in December 2026 and decisions expected in March 2027. Manufacturing and supply contracts are the thinnest area, as the reader comes from a single partner, IUL, with only a mutual non-disclosure agreement of June 16, 2026 in the data room and a supply agreement being formalized following completion of the Company's reader qualification testing, while antibodies and antigens are bought on individual purchase orders from Fortis ($2,447.50), Creative Diagnostics ($5,540) and Medix Biochemica ($5,290), with the EDDP antibody coming from a single supplier; reagents are purchased on individual orders during development, as is usual before design freeze, and supply and quality agreements will follow reagent lock at design freeze. Prototype cassette tooling is contracted to Pacific Integrated Manufacturing under a September 1, 2026 consulting agreement executed electronically by both parties, and laboratory space is provided by RAIVSDx under an April 10, 2026 facility access agreement at $5,000 per month for six-month terms that renew automatically, with each party retaining its own intellectual property; on counsel's advice the facility agreement omits IP provisions, and CARI's confidential information is protected by a separate non-disclosure agreement with RAIVSDx effective November 3, 2025. The Phase 1 design review listed the quality-system compliance and ISO 13485 status of RAIVSDx as an open item. The data room contains 16 consulting agreements and one amendment dated 2022 to 2026 (including a new EWK Consulting agreement with Eric Koehler effective November 1, 2026), built largely on a common form with invention assignment, including Abingdon Health for assay development (Phase 0 priced at $110,040), PRIA for reimbursement analysis and individual scientific and regulatory consultants, together with a Richtr accounting engagement at $1,975 per month. Advisory agreements with six advisors correspond to option grants of 10,000 to 20,000 shares each on the cap table, and several of those advisors are also noteholders. Employment documents comprise an executive agreement for the CEO and at-will agreements with invention assignment for three employees, with signed offer letters stating their compensation, a CIIAA and arbitration agreement signed by the CEO on November 6, 2026,, plus two September 2024 separation agreements, including the Fiebig agreement under which 270,833 vested options were exercised, and the Company holds an ARUP Laboratories material transfer agreement of December 1, 2025 supplying banked samples for up to 24 months, a Master Testing Service Agreement with ARUP (effective September 9, 2026; signed November 3–4, 2026; three-year term) under which ARUP will perform reference-method testing under statements of work, none of which has yet been executed, and five non-disclosure agreements. The Due Diligence Team finds the contract set orderly for a company of this size, but the IUL supply agreement, any manufacturing and quality agreements, a definitive distribution agreement and any clinical site agreement beyond the Community Medical Services memorandum are the contracts that will matter most to the plan.

Commercial and Marketing Report._intro:
CARI Health, Inc.  |  Sales and Marketing Section of the Due Diligence Report
Prepared by: TEN Capital Network  |  October 22, 2026; updated November 4, 2026
Basis of preparation: the CARI Health data room, including the Company's October 9, 2026 diligence responses, its October 27, 2026 response to this report, its November 2026 response (with Scenario 5 of the financial model), the financial model dated October 25, 2026, the Pro Forma Financial Summary (October 27, 2026), the Market Sizing Documentation (October 25, 2026) and the MedSTAT Supplies letter of intent, plus the public sources noted in the text. Facts supplied by CARI are identified as such; the assessments are the Due Diligence Team's.
[LABEL] Due Diligence Team Assessment
[CALLOUT BOX] Summary of Findings.  CARI addresses a real and well-documented gap: methadone dosing today relies mainly on patient-reported symptoms because laboratory drug levels take days to return. The plan's main strengths are a concentrated customer base, a test price set well below existing reimbursement, and a consumables model in which readers are placed at cost. Its main weaknesses are that no customer has made a purchase commitment (as expected before design freeze and 510(k) clearance), the retention benefit that anchors the value proposition is unproven, no reimbursement code exists, the only distributor (MedSTAT) has signed a non-binding letter of intent without agreed terms, and the 2032 forecast requires 26.6% penetration of the reachable pool and Medicaid coverage in 48 states. On market size, the population of US methadone patients is real and reasonably framed, but the $1.5 billion TAM describes the full OUD population and is context rather than a measure of the market for a methadone-only test. The Team considers a 2032 serviceable market of about $240 million to $330 million, and an obtainable market of about $23 million to $48 million, to be a more defensible planning range than the Company's $330 million and $84 million (the Team's range is illustrative and is built from the Company's own model parameters).
Commercial and Marketing Report.Sales and Customer Acquisition:
CARI Health (“CARI”) plans to sell a quantitative point-of-care methadone and EDDP blood test to US opioid treatment programs (OTPs), the only clinics permitted to dispense methadone for opioid use disorder. The Company counts about 2,300 DEA-registered OTPs treating an estimated 750,000 patients in 2025. The market is unusually concentrated: ten operators run 836 clinics and about 300,100 patients, which is 40% of the Company's 2025 patient estimate. This concentration is the basis of the sales plan, which uses a small direct team for the ten largest operators and a distribution partner for the remaining 1,464 independent programs.
The direct team is modeled at one representative in 2027, three in 2028, five from 2029 through 2031 and nine in 2032, with one added for each 50,000 patients beyond 100,000. The Company states that five representatives are sufficient to cover the top ten accounts. The distributor channel does not open until 2029 (40% ramp), reaches full scale in 2031, and is gated in the model by state Medicaid coverage. By 2032 about 59% of patients are expected to come through the distributor. On October 27, 2026 MedSTAT Supplies, which distributes medical products to about 1,600 OTPs and whose CEO previously operated independent OTPs, signed a non-binding letter of intent to negotiate a distribution agreement after clearance. It estimates its margin on test strips at about 18% to 20% of the strip price in the initial period, consistent with the 19% take in the model, and states that reimbursement is the main cost barrier to routine testing. No terms are agreed..
Before clearance, CARI intends to build its customer base through research channels. A 30-patient pilot study at Community Medical Services, approved by WCG IRB on October 20, 2026, is scheduled to launch on Monday, December 7, 2026 , with results expected in early 2027, a clinical validation study of about 150 patients at roughly three sites is planned for 2027, and the model sells ten research-use-only readers at cost in 2027 (about 1,000 pilot patients tested). Commercial revenue depends on 510(k) clearance, targeted for 2028 for moderate-complexity laboratories, followed by a CLIA waiver targeted for 2029. The model accordingly caps the installed base at 15 readers in 2028 and expands it only after the waiver.
### Customer letters
CARI holds 13 signed documents: 12 from organizations it describes as treating more than 100,000 patients in 39 states and a distribution letter of intent from MedSTAT Supplies. The Team reviewed each one. They are summarized below by what they actually state.
[TABLE]
Organization | Document and date | Setting | What the document states

Community Medical Services (CMS) | MOU Aug 17, 2026 | Large OTP operator | Research referral arrangement and clinic space for the pilot; no purchase commitment. Recital B is blank.
Morse Clinics (NC) | LOS Apr 8, 2026 | Small OTP operator | Willingness to collaborate on clinical trials in the NIH application; framed around the methadone/metabolite ratio (MMR).
Man Alive, Inc. (Baltimore) | LOS May 19, 2026 | Small OTP operator | Support for the PAR-25-383 translator grant application.
Western Maryland Recovery Services | LOS May 1, 2026 | Small OTP operator | Support for, and interest in participating in, the PAR-25-383 application.
Sunrise Health and Wellness (CA) | LOS May 13, 2026 | Small OTP operator | Commitment as a study site (N=60 across 22 OTPs). The author is a grant co-investigator, a relationship the Company has disclosed.
APT Foundation (Yale-affiliated) | LOS May 25, 2026 | Academic | Support for PAR-25-383; treats more than 3,000 patients a year.
Johns Hopkins Bayview | LOS Jun 20, 2026 | Academic | “Willingness to consider” serving as a site for PAR-25-446; the Company calls it less committal than the others.

[/TABLE]
[SOURCE NOTE] LOI = letter of intent; MOU = memorandum of understanding; LOS = letter of support. Source: data room, Future Customer LOIs, MOUs and LOSs.
Three conclusions follow. First, none of the 13 documents is a purchase commitment or distribution agreement, and the Company's October 9 and October 27, 2026 responses agree. Second, nine of the 12 were written to support NIH UG3/UH3 applications, and most describe research-site participation rather than commercial adoption. Several of them, including Morse, Duke and Johns Hopkins, describe the product as providing MMR-informed classification, which the 510(k) will not claim. Third, only three of the ten largest operators (Acadia, CMS and Crossroads) have signed anything. The Company states that it is engaged with all ten, but the data room does not document the other seven.
The patient figure is also a measure of reach rather than adoption. Acadia (72,500 patients), CMS (20,000) and Crossroads (9,000) account for about 101,500 of the 100,000-plus total, per the Company, and that number is roughly a third of the 2032 forecast of 291,000 patients. The Company describes this as reach (“organizations treating 100,000+ patients”) rather than committed volume. A December 28, 2025 email from the CMS Chief Science Officer, who stepped down from the Scientific Advisory Board the same week, says he wants a CARI device in all CMS clinics. The Company treats it, correctly, as an expression of interest. Dr. Sherrick is also the WCG-approved investigator for the CMS pilot, which investors should weigh when reading the pilot results.
Commercial and Marketing Report.Business and Revenue Models:
CARI uses a razor-and-blade model. The CARI Reader is sold at cost ($1,750 per unit, no margin), and revenue comes from a single-use test cassette priced at $60. Revenue therefore scales with the number of patients monitored and tests run rather than with instruments placed. The model's unit economics are as follows.
[TABLE]
Driver | Assumption | Basis and observation
Price per test | $60 | About 40% of Medicare add-on code G2077 ($151.93 in 2026). Largest single sensitivity in the model.
Tests per patient per year | 5.4 | Blend of 70% of patients at 6 tests (first year, front-loaded) and 30% at 4 tests (quarterly monitoring). The 70% weight equals assumed annual patient turnover.
Gross revenue per patient | $324 | 5.4 tests × $60.
Distributor take | 19% (model) / 20% (Pro Forma) | Applies to distributor volume only; about 11.2% blended at the 2032 channel mix. No terms negotiated; the only prior input was an informal conversation years ago about the earlier wearable product.

### Pricing and reimbursement
The Company's reimbursement advisor, PRIA, reported in September 2025 that no Medicare or leading commercial payer policy addresses quantitative therapeutic drug monitoring in opioid use disorder, and that no code specific to CARI exists. OTP payment is bundled into weekly G-code payments. The Company therefore pays for the test from the clinic's weekly Medicare bundle (G2067, $277.29 in 2026) and treats G2077, the periodic dosing assessment the clinic bills separately, as a bridge code that supports the $60 price. G2077 is not payment for the test. PRIA also noted that Medicaid rates generally run below Medicare (about 0.6 times), and that a dedicated code would require published clinical evidence, clinical society support and CMS engagement. The data room contains no CPT code application.
The price is small relative to what a clinic earns from a patient. At the Company's planning assumption of $500 a month per patient, annual testing at $324 equals about 5.4% of that revenue. The Company reports that the CFOs of Community Medical Services and Behavioral Health Group regard $60 as reasonable if retention improves by 10%, but those conversations are not documented in the materials reviewed.

Four features of the forecast matter to an investor. The 2032 step is large: patients and revenue more than double in the final year, and more than half of 2032 revenue is growth over 2031. The plan requires enrolling about 250,000 new patients in 2032, roughly 960 per business day. The Company has run its own sensitivities on 2032 revenue: a $45 test price gives $62.9 million, penetration 20% lower gives $67.1 million, and five first-year tests instead of six gives $73.0 million. A combined downside (slow Medicaid, slow distributor and penetration 20% lower) gives $56.2 million, and adding a $45 price and slower collections gives $42.1 million. These are useful, but they flex the plan around its own penetration assumption. In response to this review, the October 25, 2026 model adds a Scenarios tab: at a 15% share of the national patient universe 2032 revenue is $48.3 million and the plan stays cash positive; at 10% it is $32.2 million and needs about $2.7 million of additional capital; at 10% with a 12-month clearance delay it is $14.5 million with 2032 EBITDA of –$0.6 million and needs about $11.9 million (an upper bound, because costs are held at plan). The Team welcomes these cases. Because costs and hiring are held at plan, the Company describes this as an upper bound before it re-times the commercial build to a revised launch date.
### Clinic economics and the retention claim
The deck states that a 308-patient clinic pays CARI about $92,000 a year and gains $192,000 of new revenue, a net $100,000, from a 10% retention improvement. The derivation of the $192,000 is not in the data room. The related claim of about $400,000 of annual revenue lost to dropout per clinic is supported by a one-page Company analysis, which actually estimates $821,000 to $845,000 of lost first-year revenue for a typical 300-patient clinic, or $351,000 to $375,000 if dropouts in the first 30 days are excluded. The $400,000 figure sits inside that range. The analysis states its own limits: the retention rates are for Medicaid patients and include buprenorphine patients, the 9-month and 12-month figures are extrapolated, and the $500-a-month revenue figure is a planning assumption. The Team accepts that dropout is costly. The 73% six-month dropout figure comes from a 2026 JAMA Network Open study of 1,138 OTPs. But the data room contains no evidence that CARI testing improves retention. The Company's October 2026 evidence summary cites 25 peer-reviewed studies, mostly observational, associating faster methadone titration with better retention; the largest U.S. cohort is authored by Dr. Sherrick of CMS. That supports the clinical rationale, but the step from CARI testing to faster titration remains unproven.
Commercial and Marketing Report.Marketing Plan:
CARI's go-to-market is built on clinical pull. The Company is working through a Clinical and Scientific Advisory Board (Drs. Marienfeld and Stoller among others), patient advocates (Brenda Davis and Anita Kennedy of NAMA Recovery), and the chief medical officers of operators that distributed its provider survey. Marketing programs (ASAM and AATOD conferences, advisory boards, medical education, publications and digital) are modeled at 2% of revenue in 2028 rising to 4.5%, or $3.8 million, in 2032, with distributor co-op marketing of 1.0% to 1.5% in addition. Staffing is thin until late in the plan: a Director of Sales and marketing staff in 2028, a Director of Marketing in 2030, a Chief Marketing Officer in 2031, and clinical education specialists at one per 100,000 patients (one in 2030, three in 2032). The data room shows no dedicated commercial leader before 2028.
The positioning is clear and consistent with the evidence in the data room. Clinicians dose by self-reported symptoms, and laboratory methadone and EDDP levels take one to six days (Duke) or at least four days (Sunrise) to return. The Company's comparison shows point-of-care urine tests as qualitative only and laboratory serum tests as quantitative but slow, with CARI as the only rapid quantitative option. The Team agrees that this gap exists. The messaging, however, has three constraints. The 510(k) will cover quantitative methadone and EDDP only, so MMR cannot be promoted unless a separate De Novo is granted. Capillary (fingerstick) performance has not yet been tested in patients; earlier materials did not consistently distinguish bench whole-blood results from patient fingerstick results, and the Company has since standardized that distinction. And the product name changed several times before the Company standardized it on October 9, 2026.
The evidence strategy is the weakest link in the marketing plan. The investor deck says retention is “the outcome that matters” and the metric clinics are paid on. Yet the Company's own December 2025 evidence memorandum recommends time to stable dose, time in therapeutic range and dose-adjustment burden as primary endpoints, by analogy to prothrombin time (INR) monitoring, with retention as a secondary outcome. The August 2026 board minutes state that none of the options identified so far will produce definitive retention evidence before the Series A. Two UG3/UH3 applications ($9.5 million and about $8.65 million, with decisions expected in March 2027) would fund effectiveness studies if awarded.
The Company reports that it won a Gold award at the ISAM 2026 Innovation Day in Rotterdam on September 30, 2026. The Company received the Gold award for the top overall score; the organizers' September 5, 2026 judging rules, now in the data room, award Gold, Silver and Bronze to the three highest-scoring presentations (five categories scored 0 to 20). On exit, the Company intends to build to stand alone, expecting strategic interest at the 510(k), CLIA waiver, cash-flow breakeven and scale milestones, with in vitro diagnostics strategics, healthcare investors and OTP operators named as likely acquirers. The Company cites bioMérieux's acquisition of SpinChip (about $140 million, pre-commercial) and ARCHIMED's acquisition of ARK Diagnostics ($428 million, about 7.5 times revenue). No acquirer discussions are documented.
Commercial and Marketing Report.Provider Survey and Customer Input:
The Due Diligence Team did not conduct independent physician or advocate interviews for this section, which the SOLUtion Medical report did. The Team relied instead on the Research Collective provider survey (January 2025) and the customer letters above. The survey reached 110 medical providers at Acadia Healthcare, Community Medical Services, Pinnacle Treatment Centers, Maric Healthcare and New Season, organizations that together operate about 500 clinics in 40 states. It was a 10-minute anonymous online survey fielded between December 16, 2024 and January 15, 2025 and distributed by each organization's chief medical officer to its providers who make dosing decisions (875 invited, according to the Company; the survey report cites about 900 providers employed), of whom 110 responded (about 13%), voluntarily and anonymously. Ninety respondents reported that they understood the proposed solution, and several results are limited to that group.

The survey is a positive signal of clinical need, and its description of current practice agrees with the letters. The Team regards it as supportive but not conclusive for four reasons. Respondents chose whether to respond (about a 13% response rate), so the results may over-represent interested clinicians. They are clinicians rather than the CFOs who hold the budget. Much of the survey tested the value of a same-day MMR result, which the first product will not claim. And stated willingness to use a product is not adoption. The barriers deserve as much attention as the headline: cost to patients and lack of Medicaid or Medicare coverage were the two most frequently cited concerns, and 57% would be deterred by insufficient accuracy, while the methadone retest results to date come from banked plasma and serum samples, not fingerstick blood. The Team recommends that independent interviews with at least three OTP chief financial officers and two prescribers be completed before investment committee review.

The deck also cites a $7.5 billion therapeutic drug monitoring category, which includes 15 million patients with serious mental illness ($4.5 billion) and 5 million on cardiac, oncology and transplant drugs ($1.5 billion), with no revenue in the plan.
### Assessment of the TAM
The 5 million figure is well sourced. SAMHSA's 2024 National Survey on Drug Use and Health estimates 4.8 million Americans with opioid use disorder, NIDA's HEAL plan cites 5.7 million and calls that an undercount, and capture-recapture studies range higher. The difficulty is not the population but whether it is CARI's market. The first product measures methadone and EDDP and serves patients on methadone in OTPs. By the Company's own SAM those patients number about 750,000, roughly 15% of the 5 million. The other patients receive buprenorphine or naltrexone, or are untreated, and none of them is served by this product. The $1.5 billion TAM describes the full OUD population and is four to seven times broader than the market CARI can address with a methadone test; the Company is right to exclude it from the forecast. The Team regards the $7.5 billion category as option value for future assays rather than a market size, which the forecast also excludes.
### Assessment of the SAM
The SAM is the figure the Team considers decision-relevant, and its construction is sound in method: clinic counts multiplied by per-clinic patient census, built bottom-up from operator-reported data for the top ten and the AATOD census average of 308 patients for the rest. The Team makes four observations. First, the $330 million is a 2032 figure. The comparable figure today is about $225 million (750,000 patients at $300), so the SAM mixes a 2032 population with a 2025 base. Second, the 2025 base is at the upper end of what independent sources support (see below). Third, the 2032 population relies on OTP growth of 6% a year from 2026 through 2031 and 5% in 2032, the upper end of the 3% to 7% range the Company itself derives from 2022 to 2025 data. At 3% growth the Company estimates about 920,000 patients rather than 1.1 million. The Company's October 25, 2026 sizing shows SAMHSA directory growth of about 3% a year for 2022–2025 and faster growth at the largest operators (Acadia about 6%, CMS about 10%), so the Team still reads 6% as the upper end, with 3% as the Company's own low case. Fourth, the model holds census per clinic flat and applies the average to every DEA registrant, although the DEA count includes mobile medication units, which are unlikely to carry the 308 to 359 patients of a fixed clinic. The Company's updated sizing now values its 93 mobile units at about 100 patients each, which lowers the 2025 base to about 732,000, within the Team's range. Using the $288 net price rather than the $300 midpoint lowers the SAM by only about 4%, so price blending is not the issue.

### Assessment of the SOM
The SOM is where the Team has the most concern. The Company assumes 291,000 patients, about 26% of the national patient universe, five years after a 2028 launch, for a product that needs a new clinical workflow, a CLIA waiver for most sites, and (for the distributor channel) Medicaid coverage in 48 states. Reaching that level requires winning about 27% of the ten largest operators' patients through the direct team and about 26% of independent-clinic patients through a distributor that has so far signed only a non-binding letter of intent, which would deliver 59% of volume. Signed documents represent about 101,500 patients of reach and no purchase commitments. The Team found no adoption benchmark for a comparable new point-of-care test in the materials reviewed. The Company's own sensitivities rank penetration as the second-largest driver of 2032 EBITDA. The Team therefore considers a 10% to 15% share of the 2032 patient universe to be a more defensible planning range than 26%, and illustrates the effect below by holding the Company's price, test intensity and channel take constant.

Commercial and Marketing Report.Commercial Conclusion:
CARI has identified a genuine clinical need in a concentrated market where a small direct team can reach the main buying decisions. Its pricing is conservative relative to existing reimbursement, its commercial model is simple, and its clinical and operator relationships are real. The Team regards the sales and marketing plan as credible in design but unproven in execution. Four things have to happen for it to work: the 510(k) and CLIA waiver must arrive on time, a payer or clinic budget must carry the $60 test, evidence must show benefit in stabilization or retention, and operators must convert interest into purchases. At this stage, none of the four has been demonstrated. This is consistent with the Company's stage: the current round is designed to fund the pilot, design freeze and preparation for the second Pre-Submission, while the clinical validation study and 510(k) depend on the Series A. On purchases, the absence of purchase commitments is expected at this stage. Before design freeze there is no final product or price to commit to, and FDA policy does not permit orders for a device awaiting 510(k) clearance. Signed intent from operators treating about 101,500 patients, a distribution letter of intent from MedSTAT Supplies (about 1,600 OTPs), a pilot-study MOU and planned 2027 research-use-only placements represent strong early commercial engagement for a pre-clearance therapeutic drug monitoring test. Purchase commitments are a post-clearance milestone.
The Team considers the investment opportunity attractive to investors who accept the pre-clearance, pre-revenue profile and who underwrite the market at the lower end of the range above. Priority follow-up items for investment committee review are:

Five features of the pro forma matter to an investor. The company is pre-revenue until 2028, so every dollar spent through 2027 is funded by grants, notes and the Series A, and cumulative EBITDA losses of $11.7 million from 2025 to 2029 precede profitability in 2030. Gross margin of 85% at scale is a function of holding a $60 price against a fully loaded $7.77 cost per test; the model states that reimbursement, not cost-plus, sets margin. The 2032 year carries the exit value: revenue and patients more than double, and 2032 EBITDA of $43.8 million represents 52% of revenue, a margin the Team regards as high and entirely dependent on price and penetration holding. Operating leverage is real but back-loaded, with operating expenses at 98% of revenue in 2029 and 34% in 2032. ### Series A and Series B
If the Series A closes at $10 million in August 2027, the model's cash is $9.8 million at the end of that month, $8.7 million at December 2027 and $3.9 million at December 2028. Cash reaches its low of about $2.4 million in May 2029, one month before the $6.5 million Series B targeted for June 2029, and is $8.6 million at the end of 2029. Burn between the Series A and Series B averages about $350,000 a month. On the Company's assumptions the two rounds fund the plan to profitability in 2030 with a cushion of about $2.4 million at the lowest point, which is about six months of burn at the 2028 rate.
The Team considers this plan sufficient only on the base case and not resilient. The Company's October 25 Scenarios tab confirms the sensitivity: at a 10% share with a 12-month clearance delay and costs held at plan, the plan needs up to about $11.9 million of additional capital, and at a 10% share alone about $2.7 million. Scenario 5 (November 2, 2026), a 12-month delay at base penetration with costs and hiring held at plan, needs about $0.3 million: cash dips to about –$0.3 million for one month (May 2029) on the planned Series A and B, and EBITDA turns positive in 2031. The Company states that, if clearance were delayed, it would re-time the commercial build (sales representatives, sales, marketing and customer-support leadership, clinical education specialists and launch programs) to the revised launch date while retaining the R&D, regulatory and quality team, so the capital need shown is an upper bound. A simple Team test points the same way: if all commercial revenue slipped 12 months and spending were unchanged, about $3.5 million of cumulative gross profit expected through May 2029 would be lost, which exceeds the $2.4 million cushion before the Series B. The $20 million total also depends on the Series A closing at roughly $10 million in 2027 with no regulatory clearance, and on two pending grants of $9.5 million and about $8.65 million that are excluded from the base plan and could reduce the equity needed. Series B sizing is a bridge to profitability, and the 6.7% dilution that results is lower than a growth round would require.
[CALLOUT BOX] Conclusion on sufficiency.  The proposed $1.0 million is not sufficient to carry the business to clearance, and at $280,000 funded it is not yet sufficient to reach the Series A. An investor should treat the Seed 2 note as a bridge that buys the pilot data on which the Series A depends, expect the Series A to be required in 2027, and size follow-on reserves accordingly. The total plan of $20 million is adequate on the Company's base case but has little room for delay.

### Assessment of the valuation
The Team regards the Seed 2 valuation as reasonable to attractive for the risk, for three reasons. The $9.0 million pre-money cap is below the $10.1 million the company has raised in total (including $7.0 million spent on the discontinued wearable program) and well below the Company's own comparables, which it cites as bioMérieux's acquisition of SpinChip at about $140 million before clearance and ARCHIMED's acquisition of ARK Diagnostics at about 7.5 times revenue (neither verified by the Team). Secondary summaries of Carta and PitchBook-NVCA data put the median seed post-money valuation at about $24 million (Q4 2025) and median Series A pre-money at about $48 million to $62 million (Q1 2025 to Q1 2026); those medians are software-weighted and not directly comparable to a pre-clearance therapeutic drug monitoring test, but they show that a $10 million post-money seed sits at the low end of the market. The note carries a cap, a discount, 6% interest and warrants, so its terms favor the investor.
The planned Series A at $45 million pre-money is a different matter. It is a 5 times step-up from the cap in about a year, for a company that will be pre-revenue and pre-clearance, with a prototype that has been tested on banked samples rather than fingerstick blood. It is close to the cited Series A median, but medians reflect companies with revenue. The Team views $45 million as a target contingent on pilot data and grant outcomes rather than an expectation, and the table above shows that returns to Seed 2 remain strong at $25 million. An investor in the Series A should expect to be offered a lower price if the pilot is delayed or clearance risk remains high.

[CALLOUT BOX] Entry price: the $9.0 million pre-money cap ($1.169 per share) is the lowest price the Company has offered to outside investors and sits well below the assumed Series A price, with 6% interest and 25% warrant coverage on top.
[CALLOUT BOX] Grant-funded development: NIH funding of $2.84 million supports the point-of-care platform, with $1.97 million of award backlog drawn through June 2027, so private capital funds only the part grants do not cover.
[CALLOUT BOX] Capital efficiency to date: cash has held near $200,000 for three years and the company carries no bank debt.
[CALLOUT BOX] Unit economics: a $60 price against a $3 to $8 cost per test gives a high consumables margin, with readers sold at cost to lower the clinic's upfront cost.
[CALLOUT BOX] Early profitability: the model reaches positive EBITDA in 2030 on $17.9 million of revenue, with NOL carryforwards of $2.5 million (federal) and $3.5 million (California) available.
[CALLOUT BOX] Transparent model: the Company publishes sensitivities, ties the model to its statements, and corrected the discrepancies the diligence review identified.
[CALLOUT BOX] Upside not in the plan: two pending grant applications ($9.5 million and about $8.7 million), adjacent indications, ex-US markets, additional medications, a retention benefit, and strategic interest at clearance are excluded.
Financial Report.Risks When Investing:

[LABEL] Due Diligence Team Assessment
[CALLOUT BOX] Summary of Findings.  What is differentiated. CARI is developing a quantitative, multiplex, fingerstick test for methadone and its metabolite EDDP read in about 15 minutes. FDA's own pre-submission minutes state that FDA has not previously cleared a quantitative measurement of either analyte from capillary whole blood, and that existing methadone and EDDP tests are qualitative or semi-quantitative and mostly urine-based. The differentiators are a patent-pending method that keeps the two assay signals from interfering with each other, an integrated hematocrit correction that avoids a centrifuge, and a low-cost lateral-flow format on a commercial reader. Technology risk. The strongest data are from plasma and serum samples pipetted into an off-the-shelf cassette. The product will use fingerstick whole blood, dried reagents, a custom cassette and adapted reader software, none of which has been tested together in patients. The principal risks are translation of performance into that final format, accuracy for methadone at high concentrations, untested specificity, stability and reproducibility, reader software scope and a design-freeze date that has already slipped. Suppliers and vendors. The reader comes from a single partner (IUL) with only a mutual non-disclosure agreement and a supply agreement being formalized after reader qualification testing; the EDDP antibody comes from a single supplier; research-grade reagents are bought on individual purchase orders; no contract manufacturer is selected; and the supplier qualification process the Company has written has not yet been applied to any supplier in the data room.
Science and Technology Report.Technical Report:
Prepared by: TEN Capital Network
[LABEL] Due Diligence Team Assessment
The clinical need is clear and well supported. Clinicians who dose methadone today rely mainly on what patients report, because the only way to measure methadone and EDDP blood levels is a laboratory peak and trough test that needs two venous draws about three to four hours apart and takes days to return results. The Company's January 2025 provider survey (110 clinicians), a letter from an opioid treatment program physician who already orders levels, and several academic letters describe the same gap. Methadone metabolism varies widely between patients, and the Company cites a published 17-fold variation in serum levels for a given dose. A test that returns both values in 15 minutes at the clinic would change that workflow.
The technical work to date is credible and has moved quickly. In nine months of 2026 the team identified and, by its own account, resolved a cross-talk problem between the two analytes, reduced methadone variability on the bench from 11% to about 2% CV, validated a hematocrit correction, and qualified a custom cassette for methadone and hematocrit. The team is experienced; several members previously brought a quantitative point-of-care drug monitoring assay through FDA at ProciseDx. The Team's main reservation is one of evidence rather than direction. The results that support the investment thesis were produced on a format that is not the product, and the next six months are when that gap is closed or not. The Team recommends that investors treat the pilot study, design freeze and second FDA Pre-Submission as the decisive technical milestones.
[LABEL] Details Provided by CARI Health
### Technical Summary
The CARI Methadone and EDDP Assay System consists of a single-use lateral-flow test cassette and the CARI Reader. The intended use is the quantitative measurement of methadone (MTD) and its primary metabolite EDDP in fresh capillary whole blood from adults on methadone treatment for opioid use disorder, as an aid to dosing alongside other clinical signs. The cassette uses a gold-nanoparticle label and a competitive (inhibition) format, in which the test signal falls as the amount of drug in the sample rises. Both analytes are measured on one strip and read by a camera-based optical reader supplied by IUL (the iPeak reader), which converts the signal to concentrations in ng/mL. The Company is also developing a rapid hematocrit measurement from the same sample to correct for the proportion of red blood cells.
The Company positions the product as an adjunct to clinical judgment. The initial 510(k) will cover methadone and EDDP only; the methadone/metabolite ratio (MMR), which classifies patients as slow, extensive or rapid metabolizers, is not part of the initial claim and would need a separate De Novo feature submission.
### How the Technology Works
[CALLOUT BOX] Sample and workflow. A fingerstick of about 20 µL (the requirement document allows up to 50 µL) is applied to the cassette with a sample preparation step, and the cassette is read after about 15 minutes. The requirement is a read time under 15 minutes; the Company reports bench work at 10 minutes, and as little as 5 minutes for methadone, but has not documented it and keeps 15 minutes as the specification.
[CALLOUT BOX] Assay chemistry. The strip has four lines: a methadone capture line (methadone conjugated to bovine serum albumin), an EDDP capture line, a biotin-based line that captures a receptor-ligand "trap", and a control line. Gold nanoparticles carry a methadone antibody and an EDDP antibody. The reagent screen found no cross-reactivity between the two analytes' reagents in January 2026, and in February the team found signal cross-talk when both ran on one strip because the two molecules are structurally similar. A receptor-ligand step that segregates the EDDP detector from the methadone capture line resolved it in March.
[CALLOUT BOX] Hematocrit correction. Hematocrit is measured from the same sample and used to correct the result, with a bench fit of R² = 0.9917 and an accuracy of 80% to 120% with CV of 10% or less. A custom cassette was designed around this correction and qualified in September 2026 for methadone and hematocrit, with CV of 10% or less at hematocrit levels of 30%, 40% and 50%. Applying the correction in the reader software is in progress.
[CALLOUT BOX] Reader. The iPeak is a bench-top camera reader (about 2 lb, touch screen, four-hour battery) that reads two cassettes and up to seven lines each in about 15 seconds, stores 200 results and exports to laboratory systems by HL7. The Company reports that it measured stable results across four reader units over about 15 weeks.

Assessment of defensibility. The Team regards the differentiation as real in concept and in assay engineering, and as partly defensible. The first provisional application (63/806,333) claims a lateral-flow method defined by specific antigen-to-albumin conjugation ratio ranges and running buffers, which is a formulation-level protection that a competitor might design around. The antibodies and antigens are bought from commercial vendors, so a competitor could buy the same reagents. The protective features are therefore the integrated system, the signal-segregation and hematocrit methods if granted, the clinical data, the regulatory head start and the operator relationships. All patent filings are pending, none has been examined, and a formal freedom-to-operate opinion has not been obtained. A patent landscape review by counsel found no active relevant patents. A large diagnostics company could pursue the same indication, so speed to clearance is itself a source of advantage and the key technical risk is delay.

### Overall view on suppliers
The Team considers supply chain risk to be one of the three largest risks in the plan, with regulatory timing and clinical proof. The Company's own risk register at the May 2026 review assigned medium-high risk to system integration and to securing Series A funding, and rated partner selection as medium-low. The Team agrees on the first two. It disagrees on partner selection, because the reader, antibody and manufacturing partners are each single points of failure that sit on the critical path to design freeze and validation lots. The mitigations are within the Company's control and inexpensive relative to the plan: a signed IUL agreement, a second antibody source, a selected manufacturer, and completion of supplier assessments under its own SOP.

CARI Health, Inc.  |  Management Team Section of the Due Diligence Report
Prepared by: TEN Capital Network  |  October 22, 2026; updated November 4, 2026; updated November 10, 2026
Basis of preparation: the organizational chart (ORG-001 Ver B), Team Biographies (October 9, 2026), board director and individual biographies, executive and at-will employment agreements, consulting, advisory and separation agreements, the cap table (October 27, 2026), the Team Compensation History, the CEO's prior exits summary, the Fiebig offer letter, the signed McFarland, Chon and Russell offer letters and Russell salary adjustment, the CEO's CIIAA and arbitration agreement (November 6, 2026), the EWK consulting agreement (November 1, 2026), the 2026 employee handbook, board and advisory board minutes, the hiring plan in the financial model and the Company's October 9 and October 27, 2026 responses. Biographical statements are as supplied by the Company and the individuals.
[LABEL] Due Diligence Team Assessment
[CALLOUT BOX] Summary of Findings.  CARI is led by a founder-CEO with a long operating and grant-raising record and a four-person employee team (the CEO, an Operations Director, a VP of Product Development and a Senior Scientist), supported by a deep bench of consultants who previously built and cleared quantitative point-of-care drug monitoring tests at ProciseDx. The board has three directors (the CEO, a technology founder and a healthcare private equity investor) and two observers. The team is a clear strength in diagnostics development, FDA strategy and clinical credibility. Its weaknesses are concentration and depth: product execution rests on two people, the Chief Scientific Officer role has been vacant since the 2024 pivot and hiring was paused in January 2026, regulatory and quality leadership is provided by part-time consultants, there is no dedicated commercial leader before 2028, and several advisors and observers are also investors. The CEO reports reference checks on Mr. McFarland; the Team has received no background check results.
Document review covered the organization chart, team, board and advisor biographies, the employment, consulting and advisory agreements, equity holdings, board and advisory board minutes, and the hiring plan embedded in the financial model. The CEO states that before hiring Mr. McFarland he checked references with five people who had worked with him (Larry Mimms, Peter Westlake, Valerie Day, Mike Hale and Phil Bruce), all of whom recommended him; no background check reports are in the data room. The CEO's grant history agrees with the Company's grant summary and the notices of award, and his private capital raised agrees with the cap table. For the seven prior company exits the Company has provided a summary citing a public source and excerpt for each (four acquisitions as an executive and three earlier-career transactions as a shareholder and option holder), which the Team has not independently verified. The Team recommends that background checks on the CEO, the VP of Product Development, the key consultants and the directors be completed before closing.
[LABEL] Strengths observed:
The founder-CEO, Patrik Schmidle, has led CARI and its predecessor grant-funded work for roughly a decade. NIH and NSF notices of award list him as the project lead, and the Company's grant summary shows $7.38 million of awards, consistent with his stated record of seven SBIR and STTR grants as principal investigator worth more than $7 million. He has also raised $2.45 million of private capital through the 2022 and 2023 convertible notes, which agrees with the cap table. This record of winning non-dilutive funding is directly relevant, because grants fund most of the current development cost.
The technical team has relevant, hands-on experience. Judson McFarland (VP Product Development), Kevin Chon (Senior Scientist), Subha Selvaraju, Valerie Day, Chris Johnson and Mike Hale all worked at ProciseDx or its predecessor Prometheus, which brought the Procise ADL and Procise IFX therapeutic drug monitoring assays through FDA De Novo review. The data room confirms that FDA granted DEN22023 for the Procise ADL assay in September 2023. This is the closest precedent for CARI's regulatory path and is the reason the Company can credibly plan design controls, risk management and submission work with a small team.
Regulatory and quality leadership is experienced. Eric Koehler states that he has led more than 100 FDA clearances and approvals (510(k), De Novo, PMA, PMA supplements and IDEs), and he attended the April 2025 FDA Pre-Submission meeting. He is also a noteholder in CARI, which aligns his interests with investors. The clinical advisory board adds credibility with the customers CARI wants: Carla Marienfeld (UC San Diego), Kenneth Stoller (Johns Hopkins), Brenda Davis (patient advocate at Mount Sinai Beth Israel) and others who prescribe or work in methadone treatment.
The board is stable and engaged. Gioia Messinger founded and led the company that became Arlo Technologies and sits on a public company board as a qualified financial expert. Charles Patton led healthcare investing at Oak Hill Capital Partners and is an investor in CARI through a family trust. Board minutes show regular quarterly meetings with explicit risk tables, owners and action items, and the board has pushed the Company to slow fundraising until pilot data exist and to close the seed round before results are known.
The operating model is capital-efficient. The Company runs on four employees and uses consultants for specialized work, which keeps the cash cost of the team near $1.47 million a year in 2026 and 2027 (the AP budget) and allows grants to cover most of it. Intellectual property paper is clean for the people who matter: the CEO signed a CIIAA with a present assignment covering earlier work on November 6, 2026, the three other employees signed at-will agreements with invention assignment, most consultants sign a common agreement with assignment (the November 2026 EWK agreement uses a narrower negotiated form), and all nine named inventors signed patent assignments recorded at the USPTO for the PCT application.
[LABEL] Investors should note:
Key-person concentration. Product execution rests on the CEO and Mr. McFarland. Mr. McFarland and Mr. Chon are the only two authorized operators at the Carlsbad laboratory under the RAIVSDx agreement. There is no deputy for either and no written succession plan. Torsten Fiebig served as Chief Science Officer from June 2020 (offer letter dated June 1, 2020) and as a consultant from December 2023 until the 2024 pivot. In October 2025, after interviews that included board members, the board supported hiring Judson McFarland as VP of Product Development first; in January 2026 it paused CSO and CTO recruiting because of funding constraints, and the model does not add a CSO or CTO until 2028.
CEO terms. The CEO's 2022 executive employment agreement provides a target bonus of 50% of base salary and $200,000 of severance, payable over 12 months, on termination without cause or for good reason. The copy in the data room states no base salary amount and contains no confidentiality or invention-assignment covenant, although he signed the patent-specific assignments. On November 6, 2026 he signed a separate CIIAA, countersigned by director Gioia Messinger, with a present assignment of inventions, coverage of work performed before signing (for $1,000 of separate consideration), no listed prior inventions, and confidentiality and non-disparagement covenants but no non-solicitation covenant, together with a mutual arbitration agreement. Section 12 of the CIIAA describes his employment as at-will, which counsel should reconcile with the three-year term and good-reason severance of the executive agreement. The Company's Team Compensation History shows the salary actually paid: $64,656 a year in 2021 and 2022, no salary from January to September 2024, $120,000 a year from June 2025, $90,000 from December 2025 to September 2026 and $120,000 again from October 2026 (2025 total $79,968, against $76,635 in accounts payable). The Company states that no salary is deferred or accrued, consistent with the balance sheet, while the model carries a $200,000 salary line, which the Company states is the salary expected after the Series A closes; the CEO has deliberately kept his salary low to extend the runway and fund critical technical hires. The CEO also holds 3,960,000 common shares, 63.5% of outstanding and 51.4% of fully diluted shares.
Regulatory and commercial leadership is outsourced or late. The Company relies on hourly consultants for regulatory, quality, medical and much of its scientific work. Typical commitments are small: Dr. Carr is limited to seven hours a month, Mr. Koehler's November 1, 2026 EWK agreement covers up to 20 hours a month at $250 an hour ($275 from January 2027) and can be terminated on 14 days' notice, Ms. Selvaraju up to 40 hours a month and Ms. Day up to 10 hours a week. The model adds a Director of Sales in January 2028, a Chief Financial Officer in July 2028, a Chief Regulatory Officer only in August 2031, and a Chief Commercial Officer and Chief Marketing Officer in 2031. The 510(k) submission is planned for 2027, so regulatory and quality capacity will carry the most important filing years without a dedicated executive.
Execution of the pivot. When CARI changed from a wearable monitor to a lateral flow point-of-care platform, it replaced its wearable electrochemistry team with a therapeutic drug monitoring team drawn largely from ProciseDx and Prometheus, and moved development from outsourced partners to a leased bench in the RAIVSDx shared laboratory in Carlsbad, within a grant-funded budget. The former Chief Technology Officer (Adi Mandapaka) and Chief Medical Officer (Foster Carr) continue as technical advisor and medical consultant. The former Chief Science Officer (Torsten Fiebig) and one scientist (Rajesh Seenivasan, with $22,050 of severance) separated in 2024 under negotiated agreements; Dr. Fiebig exercised half of his vested options and let the remaining 270,833 expire in exchange for $10,000. Phil Bruce left in 2025. Investors should expect further role changes after the Series A.
Insider investment. Several people with the closest view of CARI have invested in the Series 2025A notes on the same terms as other Seed 2 investors: regulatory consultant Eric Koehler ($30,000, after attending the April 2025 Pre-Submission meeting), advisory board member Edward Kopetsky ($50,000), board observer Keith Richter ($50,000; the Company states he led diligence on CARI for SDAC and NuFund) and advisor Suraj Achar ($50,000, on joining the advisory board). This signals conviction; because they have a financial interest, the Team has weighed their input accordingly when assessing independence. Robert Sherrick of Community Medical Services left the Scientific Advisory Board in December 2025 to avoid the appearance of a conflict (he holds no CARI equity; his advisory option grant was canceled) and is now the IRB-approved investigator for the CMS pilot, and the Company has disclosed that a letter-of-support author is a grant co-investigator. Cove Fund also holds a conditional right to designate a director.
Documentation. Dr. Marienfeld's consulting agreement (September 2022) continues until terminated, and she received a further 20,000-option advisory grant in January 2026; the original advisory agreements for Ms. Davis, Dr. Stoller and Mr. Kopetsky expired and were replaced in 2025. Dr. Hale's consulting agreement (September 2, 2025) runs until his services are complete, although its Exhibit A schedules services through October 30, 2025 with extension by email, and Mr. Koehler's 2022 EWK agreement expired on December 31, 2023; a new EWK agreement effective November 1, 2026 (signed November 4–5, 2026) now covers his regulatory and quality work, including the second Pre-Submission, the 510(k), CLIA categorization and the QMS, and assigns to CARI the work he performed after December 31, 2023. Unlike the common form, it assigns only inventions arising directly from the services, leaves EWK's pre-existing materials with EWK under a limited license, limits confidentiality to five years after termination, caps liability at the fees for the services concerned and has CARI indemnify EWK for product-liability claims. Signed offer letters are now in the data room for Mr. McFarland (October 8, 2025: $225,000, 152,000 options, start November 6, 2025), Mr. Chon (May 1, 2026: $125,000, 50,000 options, start June 1, 2026) and Ms. Russell (January 3, 2024: $66,600), together with Ms. Russell's salary adjustment to $100,000 effective January 3, 2023 (e-signed September 21, 2023). The terms agree with the Team Compensation History, but Mr. McFarland's letter specifies 152,000 options against the 157,000 granted, Mr. Chon's June 1 start date differs from the May 2026 start reported elsewhere, and the later salary reductions are not documented in writing. The Company's 2026 employee handbook (58 pages) is in the data room and covers California and San Diego leave and wage rules, confidentiality, conflicts of interest, AI-tool use and workplace-violence prevention; the Team noted no material issues; the data room holds no performance management system or hiring plan beyond the model.
[LABEL] Pre-funding recommendations
[CALLOUT BOX] Obtain background checks on the CEO, the VP of Product Development and the two directors (the CEO's McFarland reference checks and the sourced prior-exits summary have been provided).
[CALLOUT BOX] Amend the CEO's agreement to state his base salary and the terms on which the severance and bonus would be paid, add a non-solicitation covenant and reconcile the at-will statement in his CIIAA with the executive agreement (salary paid since 2021 and the absence of deferred salary are now documented, and the CEO signed a CIIAA with confidentiality and invention-assignment terms on November 6, 2026, using a form approved by unanimous written consent of the board).
[CALLOUT BOX] Retention grants are in place for Mr. McFarland (157,000 ISOs, granted January 11, 2026, vesting four years from November 6, 2025; his offer letter specified 152,000 options) and Mr. Chon (50,000 ISOs, granted July 1, 2026); consider written retention terms for the consultants who are critical to design freeze and the 510(k): Ms. Selvaraju, Ms. Day, Mr. Johnson, Dr. Hale and Mr. Koehler.
[CALLOUT BOX] Confirm the board structure the Series A will require, including the number of seats, the Cove Fund designation right and whether an independent director will be added.
[LABEL] Post-funding recommendations
[CALLOUT BOX] Hire a full-time head of regulatory and quality, or a CSO with that remit, before the 2027 clinical validation study and 510(k) submission, instead of waiting for the model's 2028 to 2031 dates.
[CALLOUT BOX] Add a commercial leader before the Director of Sales in 2028, to build operator relationships and the reimbursement plan, and a finance lead (controller or part-time CFO) to replace outsourced accounting as the Company approaches revenue.
[CALLOUT BOX] Put the advisory board on current agreements with defined deliverables and meeting commitments, and record how each advisor's investor status is disclosed.

Formation and charter
CARI Health, Inc. is a Delaware corporation formed on the filing of a Certificate of Incorporation dated September 17, 2021 (the data room file is labeled September 16, 2021). The certificate authorizes 10,000,000 shares of $0.00001 par value stock, consisting of 6,000,000 common and 4,000,000 preferred. All preferred shares are designated "Series Founder Preferred Stock" with an original issue price of $0.594. The preferred terms are simple: a one-times liquidation preference that is the greater of the original issue price or the as-converted amount (that is, non-participating), deemed liquidation treatment for mergers and for a sale or exclusive license of all or substantially all assets or intellectual property, voting on an as-converted basis, optional and mandatory conversion, and pro rata dividends. The certificate contains no price-based anti-dilution adjustment, no preferred protective provisions and no redemption right. Articles IX and X eliminate director liability to the extent Delaware permits and provide mandatory indemnification of directors and officers. That original charter has since been restated three times; the current Third Amended and Restated Certificate (filed August 15, 2025) is described below.
The current charter. The Delaware Secretary of State has certified (October 26, 2026) that the documents on file are the 2021 Certificate of Incorporation and Certificate of Conversion and restated certificates filed July 9, 2024, November 19, 2024 and August 15, 2025, and has issued a certificate of good standing confirming annual reports filed and franchise taxes paid. The Third Amended and Restated Certificate authorizes 8,216,000 common and 1,750,605 preferred shares, designated as 1,653,586 Series Seed I and 97,019 Series Seed II, so every authorized preferred share is issued.
