Intellectual Property Report._intro:
CARI Health, Inc.  |  Intellectual Property Section of the Due Diligence Report
Prepared by: TEN Capital Network  |  October 22, 2026; updated November 4, 2026; updated November 10, 2026
Basis of preparation: the patent filing receipts, the patent assignments for all four filings and the USPTO recordation notices (including 64/067,115, recorded June 5, 2026, and 64/122,780, recorded October 24, 2026), the RAIVSDx non-disclosure agreement (November 3, 2025), the PCT notifications, the first and third provisional applications (read from scanned images), consulting, advisory, employment, facility and non-disclosure agreements, NIH notices of award, the Phase 1 design review, the financial model and the Company's October 9 and October 27, 2026 responses. The text of the second provisional application (64/067,115) is still not in the data room. This is a diligence review, not a legal opinion or a freedom-to-operate analysis.
[LABEL] Due Diligence Team Assessment
### IP Review Summary
CARI Health has begun to build a layered patent position early and has documented ownership carefully for most of it. Within 14 months it filed four patent applications in three families: an assay family (US provisional 63/806,333, filed May 15, 2025, and the PCT application PCT/US2026/028473, filed on the last day of the priority year), a multiplex signal-segregation family (US provisional 64/067,115, filed May 15, 2026) and a whole-blood hematocrit-correction family (US provisional 64/122,780, filed July 30, 2026). All named inventors on all four filings have signed assignments to CARI, and each assignment is recorded at the USPTO (PCT family August 18, 2026; 64/067,115 June 5, 2026; 64/122,780 October 24, 2026). The hematocrit filing is drafted as a platform claim that is not limited to methadone, which gives it value beyond the first product.
The protection is early and, in places, thin. No application has been examined and no patent has issued, so the breadth of protection is not known. The assay claims are defined by formulation parameters (antigen-to-albumin conjugation ratios and named running buffers) that a competitor may be able to design around. The antibodies and antigens are commercial catalog reagents, the reader and its software belong to a vendor, and the PCT application will be published around November 2026 and will disclose the formulation details. Patent counsel completed a patent landscape review and found no active, relevant patent documents; consistent with common practice, a formal freedom-to-operate opinion will be commissioned after design freeze (December 2026, possibly Q1 2027), and no written analysis is in the data room. The Team considers the portfolio a credible foundation that will become valuable only if the pending claims survive examination, and recommends that investors treat trade secrets, data and speed to market as co-equal sources of advantage.
[CALLOUT BOX] Assessment at a glance.  Strengths: early priority date; three complementary families; a platform-level hematocrit claim; complete signed assignments for all four filings, recorded at the USPTO; invention-assignment language in the employee, consultant and advisor agreements, now including the CEO's CIIAA of November 6, 2026; a landscape review that found no blocking patents; and non-dilutive NIH funding that is properly disclosed. Weaknesses a competitor may exploit: unexamined claims defined by design-around-able parameters; commercially available reagents; a vendor-owned reader and software; imminent publication of the formulation details; no formal freedom-to-operate opinion yet; government rights; and no trademark protection.
### Detailed IP Review
The patent filings were prepared and filed by Procopio, Cory, Hargreaves & Savitch LLP in San Diego (registered attorney Robert T. Ramos) under docket numbers 132621-0010, 0011 and 0012. The Company's stated filing strategy is to protect the assay method and device, the multiplex arrangement that keeps the methadone and EDDP signals from interfering with each other, and the hematocrit-corrected whole-blood format. The cover sheets state that the inventions were made with United States Government support under NIH grant U44 DA059627. No trademark, copyright or domain registrations were provided other than the carihealth.com domain used in Company email, and no licenses to or from third parties exist in the data room.
The Phase 1 design review of May 18, 2026 records that an IP lawyer "conducted a patent landscape analysis and found no active, relevant patent documents"; the Company's October 9, 2026 change of wording to "landscape review completed" aligned the terminology and did not reflect a change in the work performed. A formal freedom-to-operate opinion is normally commissioned at or after design freeze, because it must analyze the final design; the Company plans to commission one then. No search report, claim chart or written opinion is in the data room, and counsel at Procopio has offered to review the landscape findings with the Committee in a privileged session, which the Team recommends.
CARI Health Trademarks:
CARI Health has not filed any trademark applications in the United States or elsewhere, so it holds no registered or pending marks. It uses the name "CARI Health," a "CARI" logo and the product names "CARI Methadone and EDDP Assay System" and "CARI Reader." The product name changed several times (CARI Metabolic Assessment System or CMAS, CMEAS and CARI MTD and EDDP Assay System) before the Company standardized it on October 9, 2026, and the earlier names remain in submitted grant applications and in the FDA Pre-Submission file number title. The Company uses the domain carihealth.com.

[/TABLE]
Assignments to CARI Health, Inc. are in the data room for all three families and are recorded at the USPTO. For the assay family, seven inventors signed assignments of the provisional between July 10 and July 28, 2025, and nine inventors signed the PCT assignment between May 26 and August 1, 2026; the PCT assignment was recorded at the USPTO on August 18, 2026 (reel/frame 75693/0471). For the signal-segregation family, Judson McFarland and Kevin Chon signed an assignment on May 28, 2026, recorded June 5, 2026 (Reel/Frame 74872/0405). For the hematocrit family, Judson McFarland, Kevin Chon, Chris Johnson (personally) and Corey Dambacher signed an assignment on October 12, 2026, recorded October 24, 2026 (Reel/Frame 76493/0982). The Company states that its original Abingdon consulting agreement, effective October 9, 2024, assigns inventions to CARI and covers work done before it was signed, and the original agreement has now been added to the data room.
Each application is summarized below.
US 63/806,333 and PCT/US2026/028473: Point-of-Care Methadone and EDDP Quantification Systems and Methods
Inventors: Phil Bruce, Foster Carr, Patrik Schmidle, Amanda Nicholl, Abbas Din, Tom Lee and Nina Garrett (the PCT application adds Judson McFarland and Kevin Chon). Nicholl, Din, Lee and Garrett are Abingdon Health personnel resident in Nottingham, United Kingdom. The specification states that the invention was made with Government support under NIH award DA059627 and that the Government has certain rights. The applications describe rapid lateral-flow systems and methods for quantifying methadone and EDDP in blood or plasma, including multiplex test strips that measure both analytes. The claims of the provisional include a method of quantifying methadone, a method of quantifying EDDP, test systems and lateral-flow strip devices. Each independent claim recites a labeled anti-methadone or anti-EDDP antibody upstream of a detection zone that carries an immobilized methadone-BSA or EDDP-BSA conjugate, and defines the conjugate by a conjugation ratio (at or below 100:1 down to 1:1), with dependent claims reciting six named running buffers and the multiplex form. Provisional claims are not examined. The PCT application has an international filing date of May 15, 2026 and a priority date of May 15, 2025. The international search report and written opinion are not in the data room.
US 64/067,115: Ligand-Receptor-Mediated Segregation of Detection Elements in Sequential Flow Multiplex Assays
Inventors: Judson McFarland and Kevin Chon. The title and the Company's technical record indicate that this filing covers the "trap" arrangement that resolved the cross-talk between the methadone and EDDP signals in March 2026 (a biotin-based receptor-ligand step that keeps the EDDP detector from the methadone capture zone). The filing itself is not in the data room, so the Team could not review its claims or whether the same subject matter is also in the PCT application.
US 64/122,780: Integrated Whole Blood Processing System with Controlled Red Blood Cell Partitioning for Hematocrit-Corrected Analyte Measurement
Inventors: Judson McFarland, Chris Johnson, Kevin Chon and Corey Dambacher. Claim 1 recites an integrated diagnostic system with a cassette that has a sample application region, a controlled red blood cell partitioning architecture of several partitioning zones, a hematocrit measurement zone inside that architecture and a downstream analytical region that receives substantially red blood cell-free plasma, together with an analyzer with an optical system that images both the hematocrit zone and the analytical region, and a processor that determines hematocrit from a calibration relationship and applies it to correct the analyte result. Dependent claims add a three-zone arrangement (primary, intermediate and terminal red blood cell zones), a single imaging device, two optical windows, calibration by curve, regression, five-parameter logistic function or machine learning, and sample qualification. The claim is not limited to methadone, and the specification also describes hematocrit-corrected nucleic acid detection. The claim also requires an analyzer and processor, which in the current product are the vendor's reader and software.
Other Subject Matter Acquired or Licensed
CARI has not licensed any intellectual property in or out, according to the documents provided. Prior grants awarded before September 2021 (NIH R41 and R44 and NSF awards) were made to Mentor on the Go, LLC, which converted into CARI Health, Inc. in September 2021, so any intellectual property from that work remains with CARI without a separate assignment; no patents from the earlier wearable program are in the data room. NIH funding under U44 DA059627 (total $2,835,436 over three budget periods) and the pending UG3/UH3 applications carry the standard federal rights, including a government license to inventions made with the funding, invention reporting through the NIH reporting system and a final invention statement. The Company's Material Transfer Agreement with ARUP Laboratories (December 1, 2025) supplies banked samples and the Abingdon agreement grants CARI a perpetual license to any pre-existing inventions Abingdon incorporates.
Trade Secrets
The Company's most valuable unpatented assets are assay formulations, the reagent and buffer parameters not claimed, hematocrit and concentration calibration data and algorithms, the cassette design and the clinical sample data. These are held in the quality system (documents are controlled and marked "Confidential & Proprietary"), in the RAIVSDx laboratory in Carlsbad and with outside partners. The CEO signed a CIIAA on November 6, 2026, and employees (McFarland, Chon and Russell) have signed at-will agreements with confidentiality and present assignment of inventions, consultants sign a common agreement with assignment and confidentiality, and the Company has non-disclosure agreements with RAIVSDx (November 3, 2025, one-way in CARI's favor), IUL (June 16, 2026), DCN Dx (September 20, 2024) and two individuals (January 23 and September 3, 2026). The Team notes two remaining gaps (a third, the CEO's agreement, was closed on November 6, 2026). The RAIVSDx facility agreement omits IP provisions on counsel's advice and leaves confidentiality to the separate NDA, whose use limit is framed around evaluating a business opportunity; IP terms for any collaborative project are to be set by separate agreement. The IUL agreement protects oral disclosures only if they are marked and summarized in writing within 30 days and contains a clause allowing use of information retained in unaided memory. The CEO's executive employment agreement contains no confidentiality or invention-assignment covenant, but his November 6, 2026 CIIAA now supplies both and covers work performed before signing. And the PCT publication will place the claimed formulation details in the public domain.
Copyrights
No copyright registrations were provided. The reader software, firmware and its documentation are owned by IUL; CARI's own software is limited to analysis parameters and methods (assay method files and curve-fit parameters) that run on the vendor's reader. CARI's requirement documents, design history file and reports are created under consulting and employment agreements with assignment language.

Competition Report._intro:
CARI Health, Inc.  |  Competition Section of the Due Diligence Report
Prepared by: TEN Capital Network  |  October 22, 2026; updated November 4, 2026
Basis of preparation: CARI Health documents (investor deck, FDA Pre-Submission minutes, PRD-001 and CID-001 competitor tables, provider survey, letters of support, board minutes, financial model) and public sources retrieved on October 22, 2026, listed at the end of this report. Public information on private competitors is limited; where no customer feedback or sales data was found, the report says so. Threat ratings and outlooks are the Due Diligence Team's judgments.
[LABEL] Due Diligence Team Assessment
[CALLOUT BOX] Summary of Findings.  CARI's competition is not another methadone blood test; none that is cleared and available was found. FDA stated in the April 2025 Pre-Submission minutes that no quantitative methadone or EDDP measurement from capillary blood has been cleared, and that existing methadone tests are qualitative or semi-quantitative and mostly urine-based. CARI competes instead for the clinic's existing ways of managing dose: clinical judgment (the largest competitor), reference laboratory blood testing, urine drug testing from point-of-care cups and from laboratories, and, later, other point-of-care platforms that could add methadone. The Team rates the status quo as the strongest competitor and the best-funded point-of-care platform owners (ProciseDx under Biosynex, SpinChip under bioMérieux, and ARK Diagnostics under ARCHIMED) as the most important future threats. CARI's opportunities are a clear gap in the market, a 2024 federal rule that lowers reliance on toxicology results for take-home decisions, a concentrated customer base, and active strategic buying in point-of-care diagnostics. The Team's main concern is speed: the advantage is clear but unprotected by cleared products, and a larger company that decided to enter could do so while CARI waits for clearance in 2028.
Competition Report.Competitive Landscape:
A methadone clinic can obtain information about a patient's methadone exposure in four ways. It can rely on the patient's report and clinical judgment. It can send blood to a reference laboratory for a peak and trough test. It can test urine on site with a rapid cup or send urine to a laboratory. Or it can, in future, use a point-of-care blood test such as CARI's. CARI's competitors therefore fall into five groups, and the Team profiles ten of them.
[TABLE]
Group | Examples profiled | What they measure | Role in an opioid treatment program
Status quo | Clinical judgment and patient report | Symptoms, self-report | Default basis for dose changes
Reference and specialty laboratories | ARUP (and laboratories that refer to it); Aegis Sciences; Millennium Health | Methadone and EDDP by LC-MS/MS in blood or urine | Confirmation and compliance testing; rarely used for dosing
Urine immunoassays | Abbott (Alere iCup); Lin-Zhi International on automated analyzers; ARK Diagnostics | Presence of methadone or EDDP above a cutoff (qualitative or semi-quantitative) | Adherence and diversion monitoring
Point-of-care platform companies | ProciseDx (Biosynex); SpinChip (bioMérieux) | Quantitative drug or biomarker levels in blood in minutes | Not yet in opioid treatment; possible entrants
Alternative approaches | Pharmacogenomic dosing (CYP2B6) and metabolic ratio research | Genotype or metabolic ratio | Research stage; not approved for dosing
[/TABLE]
[SOURCE NOTE] Market context: published estimates for the global drug-of-abuse testing market vary by publisher, with one 2025 estimate of $5.46 billion rising to $8.17 billion by 2031, and urine the largest sample type (41.7% of the market in 2025). The Company's own market is narrower: methadone patients at US opioid treatment programs.
Competition Report.Competitor Profiles:
### 1. The Status Quo: Clinical Judgment and Patient Report
[TABLE]
Dimension | Assessment
Market positioning | The default way methadone doses are set and changed. Clinicians titrate slowly, in 5 to 10 mg steps, and rely on how patients say they feel.
Product offering | No product. Dose decisions use symptom scales, patient reports and clinic experience, with occasional laboratory levels.
Strengths | Free, immediate, familiar and aligned with the 2024 federal rule, which moved take-home dosing from rule-based criteria to the treating practitioner's clinical judgment. It needs no new workflow, equipment or budget.
Weaknesses | Dosing is guesswork. In the Company's provider survey 87% of respondents said patients take three or more weeks to reach a therapeutic dose, and 79% said self-report is what they rely on most. Dropout is high (about 73% of Medicaid patients leave within six months at the median program, per the 2026 JAMA Network Open study the Company cites). Metabolism varies widely between patients.
Marketing and sales | Not applicable, but it is reinforced by training and by the safety-driven norm of starting low and going up slowly.
Customer feedback | Providers describe it as "blind dosing" in the survey and letters. 83% of surveyed providers rarely or never order peak and trough tests, which shows that clinics accept the status quo because the alternative is impractical.
Outlook | It will persist. Expanded take-home doses mean fewer clinic visits, which makes objective data more useful but also reduces the opportunities to collect samples.
Threat to CARI | High. Inertia and budget competition, not a rival product, are the most likely reasons CARI would win slowly.
[/TABLE]
### 2. Reference Laboratories: ARUP Laboratories and Peers
[TABLE]
Dimension | Assessment
Market positioning | The reference standard for quantitative methadone and EDDP in blood. ARUP lists "Methadone and Metabolite, Serum or Plasma, Quantitative" (test 0090699), a laboratory-developed LC-MS/MS test that is New York State approved. Cleveland Clinic Laboratories lists the same test as a send-out to ARUP, and large national laboratories such as Quest and Labcorp appear in market reports as major players in drug testing.
Product offering | LC-MS/MS quantitation of both analytes with a reporting limit of 10 ng/mL; CPT 80358 (alternate G0480). It needs 1 mL of serum or plasma, separated within two hours and shipped refrigerated, and is performed every day of the week.
Strengths | Accuracy and credibility: CARI uses ARUP as its comparator method. Broad reach, interfaces to electronic records, and regulatory comfort because laboratory-developed tests are not subject to FDA clearance after a federal court vacated the FDA rule on March 31, 2025 and FDA reverted the regulation in September 2025.
Weaknesses | Needs venipuncture, and a peak and trough test needs two draws three to four hours apart. Specimen handling is demanding and results take days. The Company's letters of support describe laboratory turnaround of one to six days (Duke) and at least four days (Sunrise Health and Wellness), and the Company's survey found 85% wait three or more days.
Marketing and sales | Test directory listings and physician ordering through health systems and laboratory interfaces; no specific campaign for methadone dosing was found.
Customer feedback | Clinicians value the data but describe the process as impractical. Several letters say laboratory-based levels are effectively too slow for real-time dosing. No public customer reviews were found.
Outlook | The incumbent for quantitation will remain the reference. The vacated LDT rule leaves laboratories free to launch new methods without clearance, so a laboratory could shorten turnaround or add microsampling, although it cannot become point-of-care. ARUP is also a supplier to CARI (the December 2025 material transfer agreement), so the relationship is both cooperative and competitive.
Threat to CARI | Medium. It sets the performance bar CARI must match, but is slow and burdensome.
[/TABLE]
### 3. Aegis Sciences Corporation
[TABLE]
Dimension | Assessment
Market positioning | A forensic toxicology and healthcare laboratory in Nashville, founded in 1990, offering definitive testing of urine, oral fluid and blood for pain management, behavioral health and substance use disorder programs.
Product offering | Medication compliance and drug-use testing, drug interaction assessment, specimen collection and pharmacogenetic testing, plus anti-doping and forensic services. It serves Medicare, managed Medicaid and commercial populations.
Strengths | Established relationships with substance use clinics, definitive (confirmatory) methods, payer experience and an offering that already includes blood specimens and pharmacogenetics.
Weaknesses | Central-laboratory model with shipping and turnaround, a focus on compliance rather than dose titration, and no point-of-care product.
Marketing and sales | Healthcare-specialty sales and consulting services; positions itself as providing clinically actionable information.
Customer feedback | None found in public sources.
Outlook | Likely to keep expanding pharmacogenetic and blood-based services. It controls part of the toxicology budget CARI would draw on, and could be a channel partner as easily as a competitor.
Threat to CARI | Medium-Low. A channel and budget competitor rather than a product rival.
[/TABLE]
### 4. Millennium Health
[TABLE]
Dimension | Assessment
Market positioning | A CLIA-certified, CAP-accredited laboratory with more than 15 years of experience in medication monitoring and drug testing for pain, substance use disorder, behavioral health and primary care.
Product offering | Urine drug testing (Millennium UDT) and oral fluid testing (Millennium OFT), covering more than 100 drugs and metabolites.
Strengths | Scale, clinical laboratory credentials, a payer-facing market access team and Medicare and Medicaid participation.
Weaknesses | Urine and oral fluid focus, which shows presence rather than blood level. Its own materials stress responsible, medically necessary testing and cost control, which suggests payers scrutinize toxicology spending.
Marketing and sales | Direct relationships with providers and active engagement of payers and policymakers.
Customer feedback | None found in public sources.
Outlook | Stable; its main risks are payment scrutiny and a policy shift away from toxicology-driven decisions in opioid treatment.
Threat to CARI | Low. It competes for toxicology budget only.
[/TABLE]
### 5. Abbott (Alere iCup Family)
[TABLE]
Dimension | Assessment
Market positioning | Leading point-of-care urine drug screens. Abbott, which acquired Alere, is named among the key players in every drug-testing market report reviewed.
Product offering | Integrated urine cups (iCup, iCup Dx, iCup Dx Pro and iScreen) that are CLIA-waived and give results in about five minutes. Panels include methadone (an enzyme immunoassay product code, DJR), with methadone and EDDP cutoffs of 300 ng/mL, plus adulteration checks.
Strengths | Brand, distribution through toxicology and medical distributors, low cost, simplicity, CLIA waiver and entrenched use in addiction management settings.
Weaknesses | Qualitative: it reports presence above a cutoff, not a concentration, so it cannot support dose titration. Results can be manipulated (a laboratory-medicine group notes that patients add methadone to urine, which produces methadone without EDDP), and confirmation requires a laboratory method.
Marketing and sales | Distributor-led sales of test cups and panels to physicians' offices, clinics and laboratories.
Customer feedback | No independent reviews were found. The federal rule changes of 2024 reduce the weight of toxicology results in take-home decisions.
Outlook | Stable and mature. Abbott could extend its point-of-care franchise, but no methadone blood test was found.
Threat to CARI | Medium-Low as a budget competitor, and Medium as a potential entrant with deep distribution.
[/TABLE]
### 6. Lin-Zhi International (LZI) and Automated Urine Immunoassays
[TABLE]
Dimension | Assessment
Market positioning | Cleared reagents for automated laboratory analyzers. The data room lists LZI Methadone II Enzyme Immunoassay (K192433, 2019), cleared as qualitative and semi-quantitative on automated chemistry analyzers including the Beckman AU680, and the LZI EDDP assay (K170416, 2017) for the Roche cobas c303 and c503. The Company's requirement documents use these as predicate and comparison devices.
Product offering | Urine screening reagents at a 300 ng/mL methadone cutoff, run on laboratory analyzers.
Strengths | Cleared, inexpensive, widely installed on existing platforms in toxicology laboratories.
Weaknesses | Urine only; screening or semi-quantitative; laboratory based; no dose guidance.
Marketing and sales | Reagent sales to laboratories and analyzer vendors.
Customer feedback | None found.
Outlook | Mature. Their main relevance to CARI is regulatory: FDA noted that these devices are semi-quantitative and urine-based, which is why a perfect predicate for CARI does not exist.
Threat to CARI | Low.
[/TABLE]
### 7. ARK Diagnostics (ARCHIMED)
[TABLE]
Dimension | Assessment
Market positioning | A Fremont, California specialist in immunoassays for therapeutic drug monitoring and drug-of-abuse testing, using its EMIT technique, sold in more than 30 countries. ARCHIMED Diagnostics acquired a 60% stake from Soulbrain Holdings in a deal valuing ARK at $428 million, announced October 28, 2025, with Soulbrain keeping 40%.
Product offering | More than 30 assays, including an EDDP assay (K182779, cutoffs of 100 and 300 ng/mL in urine) on automated analyzers; development work includes antiretrovirals and oral anticoagulants.
Strengths | Proprietary chemistry across both of CARI's target categories (drug monitoring and drugs of abuse), international distribution, a new private equity owner with capital and executive networks, and a joint venture agreement to expand products.
Weaknesses | Analyzer-dependent and laboratory-based; urine EDDP assay is qualitative or semi-quantitative; no point-of-care format was found.
Marketing and sales | Sells assays to laboratories and analyzer platforms; new owner emphasizes international expansion and new assays.
Customer feedback | None found beyond the transaction announcements.
Outlook | Likely to widen its therapeutic drug monitoring menu with new capital. A blood methadone assay on its platform would still be laboratory-based.
Threat to CARI | Low to Medium. ARK is also a valuation comparable: the Company cites its sale at about 7.5 times revenue.
[/TABLE]
### 8. ProciseDx (Biosynex)
[TABLE]
Dimension | Assessment
Market positioning | A San Diego point-of-care platform company founded in 2018. Biosynex, a French point-of-care diagnostics group, acquired it in 2023 after leading its 2020 Series A. Its platform was the first to receive FDA De Novo authorization for adalimumab and infliximab drug monitoring assays (September 2023).
Product offering | A desktop time-resolved fluorescence immunoassay instrument with fingerstick whole blood, results in two to five minutes, and assays for infliximab, adalimumab, C-reactive protein and fecal calprotectin. In the UK, NICE reported a price of £7,500 for the analyzer and £5 to £47.50 per assay.
Strengths | A cleared quantitative point-of-care therapeutic drug monitoring platform and the closest regulatory precedent to CARI, a corporate parent focused on point-of-care and drug monitoring, and experienced staff. Six CARI team members previously worked there.
Weaknesses | Its first menu is for inflammatory bowel disease, not opioid treatment. NICE noted no evidence on prospective use of the platform in clinical care and a limitation that it does not measure anti-drug antibodies.
Marketing and sales | Distribution through Biosynex and direct selling to gastroenterology practices; NICE experts said it returns results faster than standard care.
Customer feedback | Limited. NICE found comparable accuracy to laboratory assays in validation studies and faster results; US customer reviews were not found.
Outlook | Biosynex has said it sees many potential areas of expansion for the technology. The Team regards methadone as a plausible, but not announced, future assay, and notes that the same platform expertise sits at CARI.
Threat to CARI | Medium, rising. The most credible strategic competitor if it chooses to enter, and a possible acquirer of CARI.
[/TABLE]
### 9. SpinChip Diagnostics (bioMérieux)
[TABLE]
Dimension | Assessment
Market positioning | A Norwegian point-of-care immunoassay company that bioMérieux agreed to acquire on January 13, 2025 for an enterprise value of €138 million ($140.8 million). The Company cites this as a comparable for a pre-commercial diagnostics exit.
Product offering | A spinning-disk analyzer that delivers results from whole blood in 10 minutes, starting with high-sensitivity troponin I, NT-proBNP and D-dimer. The first product launch is expected in 2026.
Strengths | Whole-blood immunoassay with laboratory-level sensitivity, the backing of a global IVD company and its commercial infrastructure, which the CEO said it would use at no additional cost.
Weaknesses | Focused on acute and cardiac care; no drug monitoring or opioid treatment assays announced.
Marketing and sales | Will be sold through bioMérieux's point-of-care channels.
Customer feedback | None found; product not yet launched.
Outlook | Will broaden its menu after launch. Its relevance is as a precedent: large diagnostics companies are paying for point-of-care immunoassay platforms.
Threat to CARI | Low as a competitor now; moderate as a signal that strategic buyers and capital exist.
[/TABLE]
### 10. Pharmacogenomic and Metabolic-Ratio Dosing Approaches
[TABLE]
Dimension | Assessment
Market positioning | Research and early services aimed at predicting methadone requirements from genotype (CYP2B6 and related enzymes) and from the methadone-to-metabolite ratio. A published French multicentre study states that no pharmacogenetic test for methadone had been approved. Aegis, among others, offers pharmacogenetic testing services.
Product offering | Laboratory genotyping and dosing algorithms under study; the metabolic ratio (the same ratio CARI could report after a De Novo) was derived from 1,700 blood specimens in a published analysis that found extensive and ultra-rapid metabolizers make up at most about 10% of patients.
Strengths | A one-time test that does not depend on timing of the last dose, and a growing academic base.
Weaknesses | Explains only part of the variation (a 2025 study found the actual daily dose remains the most important determinant of serum level), is not real time, and has no cleared dosing claim.
Marketing and sales | Academic publication and laboratory services; no major commercial campaign found.
Customer feedback | None found.
Outlook | Likely to inform dosing algorithms. It could complement CARI (a genotype plus a measured level) or, if validated, substitute for part of the need.
Threat to CARI | Low to Medium. A substitute for the metabolic ratio feature that CARI does not plan to claim initially.
[/TABLE]

Clinical judgment | None | No | Immediate | Clinic | n/a | No

Competitor | Threat level | Timeframe | Rationale
Clinical judgment (status quo) | High | Now | Zero cost and no workflow change; CARI must prove outcomes or economics.
ProciseDx (Biosynex) | Medium, rising | 2027 to 2029 | Cleared platform, De Novo precedent, parent focused on drug monitoring; could add methadone.

[/TABLE]
Competition Report.Industry Trends:
[TABLE]
Trend | Evidence | Implication for CARI
Treatment rules favor clinical judgment over toxicology | The 2024 revision of 42 CFR Part 8 (compliance date October 2, 2024) allows take-home methadone doses from entry based on the practitioner's judgment and removes strict reliance on toxicology results. | Weakens the urine testing budget and strengthens demand for objective dosing data; fewer visits reduces sampling opportunities.
Fentanyl and higher doses | 98% of surveyed providers' patients use fentanyl alone or with heroin; 61% prescribe more than 80 mg a day; SAMHSA cites fentanyl as the driver of rule changes. | Rapid titration needs data; the unmet need is rising.
Point-of-care consolidation by large players | bioMérieux and SpinChip (€138M, January 2025); Biosynex and ProciseDx (2023); ARCHIMED and ARK ($428M, October 2025). | Strategic buyers and capital exist; also a competitive signal.
Therapeutic drug monitoring moving to the point of care | ProciseDx received the first De Novo for biologic drug monitoring assays (September 2023); fingerstick results in minutes. | Regulatory path is proven; expect other entrants.
Laboratory-developed tests unregulated by FDA | A federal court vacated FDA's LDT rule on March 31, 2025; FDA reverted the text on September 19, 2025. | Laboratories can launch fast methods without clearance; CARI bears clearance cost and time.
Drug testing market growth | One 2025 estimate: $5.46 billion in 2025 to $8.17 billion by 2031 (6.94% a year); urine is the largest sample type with a gradual shift to less intrusive samples. | Growing budget pool, but dominated by urine and laboratories.
Precision dosing research | Studies of CYP2B6 genotype and the methadone/EDDP ratio; no approved pharmacogenetic test. | Supports the clinical thesis; may add competing algorithms.
Reimbursement for definitive testing | Existing laboratory code 80358 (G0480) covers definitive drug testing; the Company's test relies on a clinic-billed dosing assessment code (G2077). | Payment for CARI's use is less settled than laboratory billing.
[/TABLE]
Competition Report.Opportunities and Threats:
[TABLE]
Opportunities for CARI | Threats to CARI
A documented white space: FDA states no quantitative capillary-blood methadone or EDDP test has been cleared. | Inertia: clinics may continue to dose by judgment and spend little on new tests.
The 2024 federal rule reduces toxicology reliance and supports clinical decision tools. | Better-funded entrants (Biosynex, bioMérieux, ARCHIMED or Abbott) could develop a methadone blood assay once clearance is shown to be feasible.
A concentrated buyer base: ten operators serve about 40% of patients, so a direct team can reach the key decisions. | Laboratories can launch uncleared tests and shorten turnaround without FDA review.
Speed and cost against the laboratory route: 15 minutes at the clinic versus days and two venipunctures. | Clearance and waiver timing: competitors have until 2028 to respond, and CARI's reader and reagents are not exclusive.
Partnership routes: reference laboratory data (ARUP), toxicology laboratories (Aegis, Millennium) and distributor networks. | Reimbursement compression, given that the $60 price depends on a clinic-billed code.
Strategic exit interest: recent transactions at €138 million (SpinChip) and $428 million (ARK) show demand for point-of-care and drug monitoring assets. | Dependence on one reader vendor and on commercial reagents, which a competitor could also source.
[/TABLE]
Competition Report.Strategic Implications:
[CALLOUT BOX] Compete against the status quo, not a rival product. Messaging and evidence should focus on time to stable dose and cost per patient, which the Company's own evidence memo recommends as primary endpoints.
[CALLOUT BOX] Protect the lead. The board has asked the Company to confirm ownership of the cassette design and assess replication risk. The Team recommends exclusive or field-limited reagent terms, a software license with the reader vendor, and prompt conversion of the pending provisional applications.
[CALLOUT BOX] Build partnerships before competitors move. Approach ARUP for reference-method alignment, one or more toxicology laboratories for distribution and reporting, and a distributor with opioid treatment program reach (MedSTAT has signed a non-binding LOI).
[CALLOUT BOX] Monitor the likely entrants. Track ProciseDx and Biosynex, SpinChip and bioMérieux, ARK and ARCHIMED, and Abbott for announcements on methadone or opioid monitoring, FDA submissions and patent filings.
[CALLOUT BOX] Use competitor transactions in investor materials with care. The SpinChip and ARK deals are public and verifiable, but neither is a methadone test, ARK is a revenue-stage business and SpinChip had not yet launched a product.
[CALLOUT BOX] Complete primary research. The Team did not interview customers about competitors. Interviews with at least three operator CFOs and two prescribers, covering current laboratory and urine testing spend, would fill the feedback gaps in this report.

Competition Report Supplement._intro:
CARI Health, Inc.  |  Competitive Advantage, Industry Overview and Completeness Review
Prepared by: TEN Capital Network  |  October 22, 2026; updated November 4, 2026
Basis of preparation: the Competition Report of October 22, 2026, CARI Health data room documents (Executive Summary and investor deck, diligence responses of October 9, 2026, evidence and reimbursement assessments, letters of support, provider survey, board minutes) and public sources listed at the end. Where a competitor claim could not be verified the report says so. Ratings are the Due Diligence Team's judgments.
[LABEL] Due Diligence Team Assessment
[CALLOUT BOX] Summary of Findings.  CARI's solution has a real and specific advantage against every competitor on one question: it is the only product designed to give a quantitative methadone and EDDP result from a fingerstick, in the clinic, in about 15 minutes. That advantage is largest against the reference laboratory route (days versus minutes, one fingerstick versus two venous draws that must be processed within two hours) and against urine cups (a measured concentration versus a pass or fail at a 300 ng/mL cutoff). It is smallest against ProciseDx, bioMérieux and ARK, which have capital, cleared platforms and distribution that CARI lacks. Most of the advantage is still designed rather than demonstrated: no fingerstick patient data exist, methadone accuracy is below target, no product is cleared, and no study shows better dosing outcomes. The Team found fourteen deficiencies in CARI's competitive position (Part D), the most serious being the absence of fingerstick and outcome evidence, methadone accuracy, the payment structure of the opioid treatment program bundle, and the concentration of documented demand in one customer. The Team also found material gaps in the Competition Report itself (Part C): thin customer feedback and sales-strategy information, no market-share or competitor price data, and omission of two industry facts, which this supplement adds (falling overdose deaths, which do not by themselves indicate lower treatment demand, and bundled payment for testing). Those gaps are addressed in this supplement where public information allows.
Competition Report Supplement.Part A. Advantage of the CARI Solution O:
The CARI Methadone and EDDP Assay System is a single-use lateral-flow cassette and a small optical reader (an IUL iPeak) that report methadone and EDDP in ng/mL from a fingerstick in about 15 minutes. The table compares it with each competitor profiled in the Competition Report. The last column states whether the advantage is demonstrated in the data room, partly demonstrated, or only designed.
[TABLE]
Competitor | Where CARI has the advantage | Where the competitor is still stronger | Evidence status of CARI's advantage
1. Status quo (clinical judgment) | Replaces symptom-based guessing with a measured blood level at the visit. Survey: 79% of providers rely most on self-report, 83% rarely or never order peak and trough tests, 87% say patients take three or more weeks to reach a therapeutic dose. | Costs nothing, needs no equipment or training, and is favored by the 2024 federal rule on clinical judgment. | Need is documented. Benefit is not: no outcome study exists, and the board noted that no option available will give retention evidence before the Series A.
2. ARUP and reference laboratories | Result in about 15 minutes versus at least 4 days (Sunrise) or 1 to 6 days (Duke). Competition Report Supplement.Part B. Industry Overview and Major Tren:
CARI sits at the intersection of five sectors. Market research estimates for diagnostics sectors vary widely by publisher, so figures below are shown as examples with their sources and should not be added together.
### 1. Opioid use disorder treatment and opioid treatment programs
[TABLE]
Item | Overview, trends and implications
Overview | The Company counts about 2,300 DEA-registered opioid treatment programs treating about 751,000 methadone patients, with the ten largest operators (836 clinics) serving about 300,100, or roughly 40%. Ownership is increasingly commercial: one analysis counted 562 programs owned by private equity-backed providers, and a 2020 survey found about 62% were for-profit. Acadia alone operates 165 comprehensive treatment centers in 33 states.
Major trends | (1) Overdose deaths are falling: CDC provisional data show about 69,000 to 70,000 deaths in the 12 months ending December 2025 or January 2026, a decline of about 13 to 14%, from a peak of about 107,900 in 2022; synthetic opioid deaths fell from about 74,000 in late 2023 to about 37,400. The decline is slowing and some states are rising. (2) The 2024 revision of 42 CFR Part 8 made take-home flexibilities permanent and moved decisions toward clinical judgment. (3) Regulatory and legal scrutiny of operators: Acadia paid $19.85 million to resolve federal and state allegations, and a senator wrote to BayMark in August 2025. (4) A policy debate about allowing methadone prescribing outside programs. (5) Retention remains poor: about 73% of Medicaid patients leave within six months at the median program (JAMA Network Open, 2026). The Company cites research attributing the decline in deaths mainly to changes in the illicit drug supply rather than reduced need for treatment (nonfatal opioid overdose EMS calls about 33% below expected from May 2023; Zhu, Donahoe and Barnett, JAMA, 2026), and notes that only about one in four adults who need OUD treatment receive medication.
Implication for CARI | Demand for better dosing tools remains because retention is poor, and falling overdose deaths do not by themselves indicate lower treatment demand: Acadia's daily census grew from about 72,000 to 76,000 and CMS expanded about 10% a year through the decline, per the Company. Industry-wide OTP growth has, however, slowed to about 3% a year for 2022–2025 (SAMHSA directory, per the Company's sizing), so the Team reads the 6% assumption (to about 1.1 million by 2032) as the upper end, with the Company's 3% case (about 920,000) as the downside. Operator concentration helps a direct sales approach but also exposes CARI to the legal and reputational risks of its largest documented customer. A policy change allowing methadone outside programs could widen or change the customer base.
[/TABLE]
### 2. Clinical toxicology and drug-testing laboratories
[TABLE]
Item | Overview, trends and implications
Overview | One 2025 estimate sizes the global drugs-of-abuse testing market at $5.46 billion, rising to $8.17 billion by 2031 (6.94% a year), with urine the largest sample type (41.7%). Participants include Abbott, Roche, Thermo Fisher, Siemens, Quest and Labcorp, and specialty laboratories such as Aegis and Millennium.
Major trends | (1) Payer scrutiny: the HHS Inspector General reported $704 million of Medicare payments for definitive drug testing in 2016 to 2020 where medical necessity was in question; CMS directed contractors to focus audits on definitive testing in 2023; Labcorp agreed to pay $14.5 million to resolve urine testing claims. (2) Bundled Medicare codes for definitive testing (G0480 to G0483) since 2016. (3) A federal court vacated FDA's laboratory-developed test rule on March 31, 2025 and FDA reverted the regulation on September 19, 2025, so laboratories may keep launching uncleared tests. (4) Gradual movement from urine to less intrusive samples. (5) Consolidation and integrated data portals that lock in clients.
Implication for CARI | Laboratories are the incumbents for quantitation and can respond quickly without FDA clearance. Payment scrutiny makes it harder for any testing product to rely on payment for volume, which favors a product positioned as a dosing assessment rather than a drug test, as CARI proposes. Laboratories are also potential partners and distributors.
[/TABLE]
### 3. Rapid and point-of-care drug screening (urine cups)
[TABLE]
Item | Overview, trends and implications
Overview | CLIA-waived urine cups and dipsticks (Abbott's Alere iCup and iScreen, AssureTech and others) deliver qualitative results in about five minutes and are sold through distributors. Lateral flow is the most widely used point-of-care technology because of simplicity, cost and speed.
Major trends | (1) Federal Part 8 language moved drug testing from detecting misuse toward a clinical, strengths-based view and allows distribution of supplies that let patients test their own drug supply. (2) Rapid devices are the fastest-growing product type in drug-testing reports. (3) Commoditization and price pressure in qualitative devices.
Implication for CARI | Cups set the clinic's expectation of speed and low cost; CARI must justify a higher price per test with dose-relevant information. The cup remains necessary for other drugs, so CARI is added to, not substituted for, the cup. Combined with bundled payment this makes the budget case the key commercial question.
[/TABLE]
### 4. Point-of-care diagnostics and therapeutic drug monitoring
[TABLE]
Item | Overview, trends and implications
Overview | Published estimates of the global point-of-care diagnostics market range from $36.9 billion (2023) to $53.1 billion (2024), with growth forecasts of 7.6% to 8.6% a year; lateral flow assays are the leading platform. Therapeutic drug monitoring is much smaller: $1.99 billion in 2025 rising to $2.8 billion by 2034 (3.84% a year) in one estimate, and $2.32 billion by 2030 in another, with point-of-care devices still a small and under-used part.
Major trends | (1) Strategic buying: Biosynex acquired ProciseDx (2023), bioMérieux agreed to buy SpinChip for €138 million (January 2025) and ARCHIMED bought 60% of ARK Diagnostics at a $428 million valuation (October 2025). (2) Regulatory precedent: ProciseDx received the first De Novo authorization for biologic drug monitoring assays (September 2023). (3) Quantitative whole-blood immunoassays in 10 minutes or less are becoming available. (4) AI-supported dosing is increasingly discussed.
Implication for CARI | The exit environment is favorable and the regulatory path has precedent, but the same signals show that larger companies are building point-of-care drug monitoring franchises, and any could add methadone. Time to clearance is the key variable.
[/TABLE]
### 5. Precision dosing and pharmacogenomics
[TABLE]
Item | Overview, trends and implications
Overview | Research on CYP2B6 genotypes, body mass, sex and the methadone-to-EDDP ratio as predictors of methadone requirements. A published French study notes that no pharmacogenetic test for methadone had been approved; a 2025 study found that the daily dose remains the most important determinant of serum level.
Major trends | (1) Interest in the methadone metabolism ratio as a single-draw alternative to peak and trough testing (about 10% of patients are extensive or ultra-rapid metabolizers in one analysis). (2) Laboratories adding pharmacogenetic services. (3) Federal research funding for point-of-care, pharmacokinetic-guided dosing, including the NIDA Blueprint MedTech awards that fund CARI.
Implication for CARI | The science supports measuring levels and the ratio, and academic sites (Duke, Johns Hopkins, UVM) have offered letters of support. A validated genotype-based approach could substitute for part of the benefit, but is not near-term.
[/TABLE]

Executive Summary of Exit Strategy Findi._intro:
CARI Health, Inc.  |  Exit Strategy Section of the Due Diligence Report
Prepared by: TEN Capital Network  |  October 22, 2026; updated November 4, 2026
The due diligence team reviewed CARI Health's exit strategy as presented in the Executive Summary, Investor Deck, Pro Forma Financial Summary, financial model (Exit Scenarios and IRR Per Round tabs), cap table, Seed 2 note documents and Board minutes, and tested it against public M&A data for point-of-care (POC) diagnostics, TDM and behavioral-health testing companies. The key findings are below.
Executive Summary of Exit Strategy Findi.Key Facts Relevant to Exit:
[TABLE]
Item | Detail (per data room, October 2026)
Stage | Pre-revenue clinical prototype; 30-patient pilot Q4 2026; design freeze targeted end-2026 (at risk)
Regulatory path | 510(k) moderate complexity (target 2028) → CLIA waiver (2028–2029) → optional MMR De Novo (2029)
Current round | $1.0M Seed 2 convertible note; $9M pre / $10M post cap; $280K funded, $120K soft circled, $600K open
Change-of-control terms (Seed 2 note) | If the company is sold before the note converts: repayment of principal plus interest, or, on election of the Majority Holders, conversion into common stock at the $9M pre-money cap
Planned future rounds (estimates) | Series A $10M at $45M pre (Aug 2027); Series B $6.5M at $90M pre (Jun 2029)
Ownership (fully diluted, Oct 2026) | Founder 51%, options/employees ~20%, Series Seed I/II investors ~23%; 7,698,766 FD shares
Revenue plan | 2028: $1.9M · 2029: $8.2M · 2030: $17.9M · 2031: $35.8M · 2032: $83.6M
Company-illustrated exit values | 2032 at 4.0x / 6.5x / 9.0x revenue = $334M / $543M / $752M; early strategic exit (Q4 2027) $75M / $141.5M / $200M
[/TABLE]
Executive Summary of Exit Strategy Findi.Key Findings:
[CALLOUT BOX] The proposed exit is a strategic sale, not an IPO. CARI's plan is to build to stand alone while positioning for acquisition at one of four value inflection points between 2028 and 2032. The base case values a 2032 exit at ~$543M (6.5x 2032 revenue). This is a sound general framework for a single-platform IVD company, but the plan has no named process, timing trigger, banker or documented strategic relationships yet.
[CALLOUT BOX] Comparable transactions support a $100M–$170M value for a POC platform that has cleared FDA but has little revenue. SpinChip (~$140M, pre-revenue), Epocal ($166M upfront) and LEX Diagnostics (~$100M at 510(k) plus CLIA waiver, pre-launch) all fall in this range. ARK Diagnostics ($428M) shows the value of a profitable TDM and drugs-of-abuse franchise at scale.
[CALLOUT BOX] Comparables also show the downside. LumiraDx's POC platform sold to Roche for $295M, with all proceeds going to lenders and nothing to shareholders. ProciseDx, the most direct analog to CARI and the former employer of much of CARI's team, was bought by its own minority investor for an undisclosed price tied to an FDA earn-out; the acquirer has since entered a French safeguard proceeding.
[CALLOUT BOX] Estimated ROI to a Seed 2 investor is attractive if CARI reaches clearance. Applying the comparable valuations to CARI's cap table and planned dilution, a $100K Seed 2 investment returns about 7x–15x in early strategic-sale scenarios (2028–2030), 10x–25x in revenue-stage scenarios (2031–2032), and 40x+ only if the full 2032 plan is achieved and valued at ARK's multiple. Failure or sub-scale scenarios return 0x–1x. The team's risk-weighted estimate is ~7.5x (~9.4x with warrants), and nearly half of that expected value comes from the 10% probability of a scale exit.
[CALLOUT BOX] Return metric definition. The earlier "aggregate investor return" divided enterprise value by total capital raised (27.2x in the 2032 base case), which is not comparable to per-investor returns. The October 25, 2026 model replaces it with an ownership-based multiple (13.1x in the 2032 base case, before preferences and fees), consistent with the Team's ~13x, and the Company's investor materials now cite per-round figures.
[CALLOUT BOX] The acquirer universe is real but in flux. Thermo Fisher, Roche, Abbott, Siemens Healthineers, QuidelOrtho, bioMérieux and ARCHIMED/ARK are credible strategic or sponsor buyers, and several are active POC buyers right now (Roche–LumiraDx, bioMérieux–SpinChip, QuidelOrtho–LEX). However, Siemens Healthineers is preparing a carve-out of its diagnostics business, Biosynex is in safeguard, and the largest OTP operators are under financial or activist pressure (BayMark debt restructuring, Acadia activist campaign). This makes OTP operators unlikely acquirers at strategic multiples.
[CALLOUT BOX] Seed and Series A investors may favor different exit timing. An early strategic sale at ~$100M–$170M returns roughly 7x–15x to Seed 2 investors but only ~1.6x–2.7x to the planned Series A. Series A investors will therefore likely push for a revenue-stage exit, and Board composition and protective provisions agreed at the Series A will shape when CARI can sell.
Executive Summary of Exit Strategy Findi.Reasons to Invest (Exit Perspective):
[CALLOUT BOX] Low entry valuation ($10M post-money cap) relative to the $100M+ value at which comparable POC platforms have been acquired at or near FDA clearance.
[CALLOUT BOX] Razor-and-blade consumable model with ~95% cassette gross margin and recurring revenue, the profile IVD strategics pay premium multiples for.
[CALLOUT BOX] Clear, near-term regulatory value inflection points (510(k) and CLIA waiver in 2028) that are the same milestones at which SpinChip, Epocal and LEX were acquired.
[CALLOUT BOX] Highly concentrated customer base (ten operators run 836 clinics and ~300,100 patients), which makes commercial traction visible to acquirers quickly and limits sales-force cost.
[CALLOUT BOX] Team has already taken a quantitative POC TDM test through FDA (ProciseDx) and the CEO has been part of seven company exits (four acquisitions as an executive and three earlier-career transactions as a shareholder and option holder).
[CALLOUT BOX] Non-dilutive funding ($2.84M awarded; about $18.15M of UG3/UH3 applications pending, decisions March 2027) reduces dilution and raises per-share exit proceeds.
[CALLOUT BOX] Large existing strategic players (Thermo Fisher, Siemens, Roche, ARK) already sell lab-based methadone and EDDP immunoassays, so CARI fills an obvious POC gap in their portfolios.
Executive Summary of Exit Strategy Findi.Risks When Investing (Exit Perspective):
[CALLOUT BOX] Exit value depends on FDA clearance and CLIA waiver that have not been obtained; design freeze has already slipped from June 2026 to end-2026 and remains at risk.
[CALLOUT BOX] Base-case exit value rests on 2032 revenue that more than doubles in the final forecast year; a one-year slip in the plan reduces the ARK-multiple value from ~$627M to ~$268M.
[CALLOUT BOX] Comparable set is thin. The two comparables CARI cites are imperfect (SpinChip addresses the much larger cardiac troponin market; ARK is a profitable, 20-year-old, multi-country company), and there is ambiguity over whether ARK's $428M is the value of 100% or of the 60% stake.
[CALLOUT BOX] Single indication with a ~$330M SAM may be below the size threshold some large IVD acquirers require, unless the TDM platform is shown to extend beyond methadone.
[CALLOUT BOX] Acquirer diligence will focus on items still open: the IUL reader supply agreement (being formalized), sole-source EDDP antibody and unproven retention benefit.
[CALLOUT BOX] If CARI is sold before the Seed 2 note converts, holders receive only principal plus interest unless the Majority Holders elect conversion; individual note holders cannot elect conversion on their own.

Exit Strategy Report.Proposed Exit Strategy:
CARI Health's exit strategy, as described across the Executive Summary, Investor Deck and financial model, can be defined as follows: build a stand-alone, cash-flow-positive POC TDM business and sell it to a strategic IVD company or healthcare investor once a value inflection point has been reached. The company does not depend on an exit to survive; its financial plan reaches profitability on $20M of total capital. The company sees four inflection points at which acquirer interest is expected to increase, and its model adds an earlier, illustrative strategic-sale scenario immediately after the clinical validation study.

FDA 510(k) clearance (moderate complexity) | 2028 | Regulatory risk retired for MTD + EDDP; sales to CLIA-certified OTP labs | IVD strategics; TDM/DAT specialists | SpinChip ~$140M; Epocal $166M upfront
CLIA waiver | 2029 (Company target; previously later 2028) | Test usable in any OTP, ED or jail setting; full addressable market opens | POC-focused strategics (QuidelOrtho, Abbott, Roche) | LEX Diagnostics ~$100M at 510(k) + CLIA waiver, pre-launch
Cash-flow positive | 2030 ($17.9M revenue, $4.2M EBITDA) | Adoption, pricing and reimbursement proven | Strategics and healthcare PE (e.g., ARCHIMED) | Model: 4.0x–9.0x revenue = $72M–$161M
Scale | 2032 ($83.6M revenue, $43.8M EBITDA) | Market leadership in methadone TDM; platform for other drugs | Large IVD strategics; PE platforms | Model: 4.0x–9.0x revenue = $334M–$752M (base 6.5x = $543M)
[/TABLE]
Source: CARI Health Executive Summary, Pro Forma Financial Summary and Financial Model (tab 7, Exit Scenarios), October 2026. Comparable references added by the due diligence team.
The plan presents three valuation lenses. Revenue multiples of 4.0x (sector median), 6.5x (base) and 9.0x (high) are anchored on KPMG's Q1-2025 Life Sciences Tools & Diagnostics data and the ARK Diagnostics transaction. EBITDA multiples of 8x / 12x / 16x are anchored on FOCUS Investment Banking data and ARK's reported ~13.9x EBITDA. A precedent-based early-exit scenario values CARI at $75M–$200M in Q4 2027, with SpinChip as the single direct precedent. The model itself flags this early-exit comparable set as "thin" and the scenario as "speculative and directional."
The Board minutes show the exit is not yet an active workstream. The Q3 2026 Board meeting focused on closing the seed round by mid-November 2026, the pilot study and the Series A. The Board rated "Series A before FDA clearance" as the highest risk and advised management to "prove the methadone indication first before broadening scope." The only partner-related action item is "explore alternative business models with partners," which is in progress with a research-use-only (RUO) path targeted for Q1 2027. No term sheets, letters of interest from acquirers, or strategic-partner discussions are documented in the data room.

Observations: SpinChip is a valid but generous precedent. It is the closest pre-revenue POC platform deal, but its troponin test addresses the much larger cardiac emergency market, it had a European multicenter study under way, and bioMérieux had already taken a minority stake about ten months before the buyout. That prior stake set a reference price, which CARI does not have. ARK is the right category comparable but a different business stage. ARK is profitable (Korean reporting cites net profit of over ₩40bn) and has a global menu. Applying its multiple to CARI's 2032 forecast assumes CARI reaches comparable maturity. U.S. reporting describes the deal as valuing ARK at $428M, while Korean reporting indicates ₩607bn (~$428M) was paid for the majority stake, implying ~₩870bn for 100%. If the latter is correct, ARK's true multiple is higher than the 7.5x CARI uses, which would make CARI's base case conservative on multiple but not on revenue. CARI's model also lists other diagnostics deal multiples: Nova Biomedical 4.8x, Akoya Biosciences 3.0x, Ambry Genetics 2.5x and Median Diagnostics 1.7x revenue, against a sector public-market median of ~3.5x. These suggest 6.5x is above the typical outcome and requires CARI's high growth and margins to hold.

Exit Strategy Report.Estimated ROI to CARI Health Investors B:
To translate each comparable into a return for current investors, the due diligence team applied each transaction's valuation (or revenue multiple) to CARI and ran the result through CARI's planned capitalization. Second, ~44% of the expected value comes from the 10% probability of a scale exit, which depends on the 2031–2032 forecast. The per-round figures in the model's "IRR Per Round" tab (e.g., Seed 2 MOIC 49x and Series A MOIC 9.2x at a 6.5x 2032 exit) are consistent with the team's figures above and are the figures the Company's investor materials now cite.
Exit Strategy Report.Strengths and Weaknesses of the Proposed:
### Strengths
[CALLOUT BOX] Multiple exit windows. Defining four inflection points gives the Board options to sell into strategic interest at clearance, at waiver, at profitability or at scale, rather than betting on one outcome. The early windows coincide with milestones at which comparable POC companies were acquired (SpinChip, Epocal, LEX).
[CALLOUT BOX] Business model acquirers value. Recurring, high-margin consumables (~95% cassette gross margin) on a placed reader are the model large IVD companies prefer, and CARI prices against existing reimbursement (G2077) rather than requiring a new code.
[CALLOUT BOX] Clear portfolio gap for incumbents. Thermo Fisher (CEDIA), Roche (cobas-compatible assays), Siemens (Syva/EMIT) and ARK already sell lab-based methadone and EDDP immunoassays for urine screening. None offers a quantitative, fingerstick, 15-minute blood test, so CARI extends their franchises rather than competing head-on.
[CALLOUT BOX] Concentrated, visible market. Ten operators control 836 clinics and ~300,100 patients, and CARI holds signed letters from organizations treating 100,000+ patients plus a distributor LOI from MedSTAT Supplies (~1,600 OTPs). Early adoption by a few large operators would be easy for an acquirer to verify.
[CALLOUT BOX] Low entry valuation and capital efficiency. The $10M post-money cap and $20M total capital to profitability, with meaningful non-dilutive funding, give early investors high leverage to a $100M+ exit.
[CALLOUT BOX] Experienced team for acquirer diligence. The product team took ProciseDx's quantitative POC TDM tests through FDA; the regulatory consultant cites 100+ FDA clearances and approvals; the CEO has been part of seven exits (four as an executive). Prior regulatory and transaction experience reduces execution risk in a sale process.
[CALLOUT BOX] Platform optionality. The same reader and assay approach could extend to a $7.5B U.S. TDM opportunity (psychiatric, oncology, transplant, cardiac). This optionality is excluded from the forecast but can widen the buyer pool and support a premium.
[CALLOUT BOX] Sensible stand-alone posture. Because the plan does not require an exit to survive, CARI is not a forced seller, which supports negotiating leverage.
### Weaknesses
[CALLOUT BOX] Exit is a principle, not yet a plan. There is no defined trigger (for example, "run a process within 12 months of CLIA waiver"), no banker or advisor, no documented strategic relationships, and no Board-level exit discussion in the 2026 minutes.
[CALLOUT BOX] Headline valuation relies on the last forecast year. 2032 revenue more than doubles over 2031, and more than half of 2032 revenue is growth in that year. Applying 6.5x–9.0x to that figure produces values ($543M–$752M) that are very sensitive to timing: a one-year delay reduces the ARK-multiple value by ~57%.
[CALLOUT BOX] Thin and imperfect comparables. Only two comparables are cited. SpinChip benefited from a larger market and a pre-existing acquirer stake; ARK is a mature, profitable company. Downside comparables (LumiraDx, ProciseDx) are not discussed.
[CALLOUT BOX] Return metric definition. The earlier "aggregate investor return" (EV divided by total capital) was not comparable to per-investor returns; the Company has replaced it with an ownership-based multiple and per-round MOIC.
[CALLOUT BOX] Named acquirers are in transition. Siemens Healthineers is preparing a carve-out of its diagnostics business (FY2026), which could delay or redirect its M&A. OTP operators are financially strained: BayMark (287 locations) carried ~$1B of debt and completed an out-of-court restructuring in October 2026, and Acadia faces activist calls for a strategic review. These operators are better positioned as customers or strategic investors than as acquirers.
[CALLOUT BOX] Narrow initial market. A ~$330M SAM for methadone may be below the threshold at which the largest IVD companies make acquisitions, unless CARI shows the platform extends to other drugs. The Board has deliberately deferred that work.
[CALLOUT BOX] Open diligence items that affect value. The reader is supplied by a single partner (IUL) under a supply agreement still being formalized. The draft gives IUL ownership of the reader IP, so an acquirer would want assignability and long-term supply rights. The EDDP antibody is single-source, retention benefit is unproven, and the MMR feature requires a separate De Novo.
[CALLOUT BOX] Investor alignment and note terms. Early-exit scenarios favor seed holders but return only ~1.6x–2.7x to the planned Series A, creating potential Board tension. If a sale occurs before the Seed 2 notes convert, holders receive only principal plus interest unless the Majority Holders elect conversion at the $9M cap.
[CALLOUT BOX] Financing risk ahead of the first exit window. The plan requires a $10M Series A before FDA clearance, which the Board rates as its highest risk. Failure to raise it would push CARI toward a distressed or sub-scale outcome.

The due diligence team reviewed the corporate, contract and deal documents in the CARI Health data room. These include the Corporate & Legal, HR & Management Team, Partnerships & Contracts, Operations, Government Grants, customer-letter and IRB folders: more than 70 documents in total.
