CARI Health, Inc.  |  Regulatory Section of the Due Diligence Report
Prepared by: TEN Capital Network  |  October 22, 2026; updated November 4, 2026; updated November 10, 2026
[LABEL] Due Diligence Team Assessment
CARI Health has engaged EWK Consulting (Eric Koehler, Quality/Regulatory Compliance Consultant) to provide regulatory and quality support for the CARI Methadone and EDDP Assay System and CARI Reader. Mr. Koehler has confirmed in writing that his experience spans more than 100 FDA clearances and approvals, including 510(k)s, De Novos, PMAs, PMA supplements and IDEs. His current engagement (EWK agreement effective November 1, 2026, up to 20 hours a month) covers the second Pre-Submission, the 510(k), CLIA categorization and the QMS. The product development team (Judson McFarland, Kevin Chon, Subha Selvaraju, Valerie Day, Mike Hale and Chris Johnson) previously took quantitative point-of-care therapeutic drug monitoring tests through FDA at ProciseDx. The due diligence team reviewed the FDA Pre-Submission record (Q250159), the company's Regulatory Strategy (October 2026), its quality management system (QMS) and design-control records, the risk management plan, IRB documentation and R&D progress reports, and assessed the regulatory strategy and the current project timeline independently.
Regulatory and Project Plan Report.Project Background:
Methadone is the most effective treatment for opioid use disorder (OUD) and is dispensed primarily through federally certified Opioid Treatment Programs (OTPs). Because patients metabolize methadone at very different rates, clinicians "start low and go slow," and it typically takes four weeks or more to reach a stable dose. Clinicians currently have two testing options. Point-of-care urine immunoassays are qualitative or semi-quantitative and are designed to detect use, not to measure dose exposure. Quantitative LC-MS/MS testing of serum or plasma is performed by reference laboratories with results returned days later. FDA confirmed in the Pre-Submission meeting that it "has not previously cleared a quantitative measurement of methadone or EDDP from capillary whole blood."
CARI Health is developing a point-of-care test system that quantitatively measures methadone (MTD) and its primary metabolite, EDDP (2-ethylidene-1,5-dimethyl-3,3-diphenylpyrrolidine), from a single fingerstick sample in approximately 15 minutes. The results are intended to support, but not replace, the clinician's dosing decisions.
Regulatory and Project Plan Report.Product Description:
### Finished Product Description
The product is an in vitro diagnostic (IVD) test system consisting of:
[CALLOUT BOX] CARI Reader: an iPeak® 4.3" lateral flow reader manufactured by IUL, S.A. (Spain) and adapted with CARI-specific assay algorithms. CARI has told FDA it believes the reader is 510(k) exempt (product code JJQ); FDA has not confirmed this. A supply agreement with IUL is being formalized following reader qualification testing.
[CALLOUT BOX] CARI Methadone and EDDP Assay: a single-use, multiplex competitive lateral flow immunoassay cassette (monoclonal anti-MTD and anti-EDDP antibodies) using a CARI-designed custom cassette. A hematocrit correction is measured from the same sample, so results reflect plasma-equivalent concentrations.
[CALLOUT BOX] Sample collection components: lancet (Unistik Pro, K222303), capillary blood collection device (Safe-T-Fill, K983517) and buffer. FDA noted that any use of these cleared devices outside their own instructions must be validated.
[CALLOUT BOX] External Control Kit: specified in PRD-003 (draft). Its regulatory route (stand-alone Class I exempt control material or inclusion in the 510(k)) has not been decided.
### Proposed Intended Use
Based on the indications discussed with FDA, the device is intended for the in vitro quantitative measurement of methadone and EDDP in fresh capillary whole blood drawn from the fingertips of adults (18+) undergoing methadone treatment for OUD with a prescribed daily dose of 40 mg or more. This includes patients recently started on methadone and patients on a stable dose, whether or not their clinical status has changed. The device is for prescription use only, as an aid in the management of OUD in conjunction with other clinical findings. The initial claim is for use in moderate-complexity clinical laboratory settings. Reporting of the methadone/metabolite ratio (MMR) was removed from the proposed indication in April 2025.
Regulatory and Project Plan Report.Regulatory Path:
FDA indicated that the device will likely be regulated under 21 CFR 862.3620 (methadone test system), a Class II regulation that already covers urine and oral-fluid methadone and EDDP immunoassays (product code DJR).¹ For a Class II IVD, there are three paths to market. They are listed from the least to the most intensive:
[CALLOUT BOX] 510(k) Premarket Notification: demonstrates that the device is substantially equivalent to a legally marketed predicate device with the same intended use, and that any technological differences do not raise different questions of safety and effectiveness. FDA's performance goal is 90 FDA review days, with clock stops for additional-information requests.
[CALLOUT BOX] De Novo Classification Request: for novel low-to-moderate-risk devices with no suitable predicate. The sponsor proposes special controls and a new classification, which typically requires more clinical evidence and a longer review (150 FDA review days).
[CALLOUT BOX] Premarket Approval (PMA): for Class III devices; not applicable to this product.
IVDs are also assigned a CLIA complexity categorization (waived, moderate or high complexity) that determines where the test may be performed. A moderate-complexity test may only be run in laboratories holding a CLIA certificate for moderate- or high-complexity testing. A CLIA waiver allows use in any setting with a Certificate of Waiver, including most OTP dosing areas. A waiver requires a separate application showing the test is simple and has an insignificant risk of an erroneous result in the hands of untrained, intended operators. It can be sought after 510(k) clearance (CLIA Waiver by Application) or together with the 510(k) (Dual 510(k) and CLIA Waiver by Application).²
Regulatory and Project Plan Report.Regulatory Strategy:
CARI's strategy is to obtain the least burdensome, predicate-based clearance first and then expand the claims and settings in steps:
[TABLE]
Phase | Regulatory action | Market enabled | Company target
1 | 510(k) for quantitative MTD and EDDP from capillary whole blood (moderate complexity) | OTPs and laboratories with moderate-complexity CLIA certificates | Clinical validation study and 510(k) submission 2027; clearance 2028
2 | CLIA waiver for MTD and EDDP | CLIA-waived and point-of-care settings across the broader OTP market | 2028–2029 (Company target; previously later 2028)
3 (optional) | De Novo to add MMR reporting | MMR as a labeled clinical decision metric | 2029, if clinical evidence supports it
4 (exploratory) | AI-guided dosing recommendations | Decision-support layer on longitudinal data | Not scheduled
[/TABLE]
Source: CARI Health FDA Communications Summary & Regulatory Strategy, October 2026.
The candidate predicates discussed with FDA are K192433 (LZI Methadone II enzyme immunoassay, urine, 300 ng/mL cutoff) and K023617 (Microgenics EDDP assay, urine). CARI's Product Requirements Document also references K170416 (LZI EDDP) and K182779 (ARK EDDP). All are qualitative or semi-quantitative urine assays run on clinical chemistry analyzers, so CARI must use analytical performance data and a capillary-to-venous comparison to show that the differences do not raise new questions of safety and effectiveness. The due diligence team considers this sequencing appropriate. Removing MMR from the initial claim converted a likely De Novo into a probable 510(k), and commercial launch depends only on Phase 1. A Phase 4 dosing-recommendation feature would likely be regulated as device software and would need its own regulatory assessment.
Regulatory and Project Plan Report.Completed Activities:
[CALLOUT BOX] Pre-Submission Q250159 was submitted on January 21, 2025 (FDA acknowledgement on file). CARI answered FDA's interactive-review questions on March 10, 2025, and FDA issued written feedback in March 2025 (dated March 27, 2025, per the company).
[CALLOUT BOX] A one-hour teleconference was held on April 3, 2025 with the CDRH Division of Chemistry and Toxicology Devices, a CDRH medical officer, CDER representatives and NIDA program officials. CARI's draft minutes were submitted as amendment Q250159/A001 (received April 8, 2025). The minutes in the data room show FDA's tracked edits, a routine part of the Pre-Submission process; for example, "voiced support for that revised path" was changed to "this approach seemed reasonable."
The written feedback and meeting addressed the following:
[CALLOUT BOX] 510(k) pathway may be pursued
CARI had proposed a De Novo. FDA responded that the device will likely fall under 21 CFR 862.3620 and that a 510(k) citing an appropriate predicate may be possible if CARI shows that differences (quantitative result, capillary blood, instrument read) do not raise new questions of safety and effectiveness. FDA acknowledged that no perfect predicate exists and recommended a single primary predicate, supported by reference devices and preferably a recent one. FDA does not require a head-to-head comparison with the predicate; accuracy is to be compared with a quantitative reference method (LC-MS/MS).
[CALLOUT BOX] MMR excluded from the initial submission
FDA found the published evidence (McCarthy et al., 2020) inadequate to establish the clinical validity of MMR. CARI removed MMR from the indication, and FDA noted this approach "seemed reasonable" and encouraged CARI to collect MMR data during feasibility and clinical validation studies for a future submission.
[CALLOUT BOX] Indications for use
FDA asked CARI to define the patient population (induction and/or stable dosing), state that the test is prescription-only, list the system components, and avoid any labeling that contradicts methadone drug labeling (i.e., no dosing instructions). FDA had no further comments on the revised indication.
[CALLOUT BOX] Comparator method
A validated U.S. LC-MS/MS method (for example ARUP Laboratories' CAP/CLIA/ISO 15189 laboratory-developed test) is acceptable in principle if validation documentation is provided. FDA cautioned that discordant results will generally be resolved in favor of the reference method, so the reference laboratory must be chosen carefully. CARI has since signed a three-year Master Testing Service Agreement with ARUP (effective September 9, 2026), which excludes GCP and 21 CFR Part 11 unless a statement of work provides otherwise; the statement of work for the validation study should add those requirements.
[CALLOUT BOX] Performance criteria and benefit–risk
FDA described CARI's proposed ±20% CV target as "broader than typically seen" for quantitative assays. It asked for clinician input and a benefit–risk analysis comparing dosing decisions made without any drug-level data (the current standard of care) against decisions using data with the device's expected variability. FDA also asked CARI to consider performance at peak and trough levels and other medical decision points.
[CALLOUT BOX] Sample matrix
Because capillary whole blood is a new matrix for this device type, FDA requires precision to be demonstrated on capillary samples (e.g., two fingersticks from different fingers of the same subject). It recommended building capillary, venous and plasma equivalence into the method-comparison study. Retrospective plasma or serum samples may only supplement prospective fingerstick samples, and accuracy data should be collected prospectively.
[CALLOUT BOX] Clinical study design
FDA did not accept the proposed 150-subject sample size without a statistical justification covering the full measuring range, the induction and maintenance populations, and ultra-rapid and ultra-slow metabolizers. It asked that interference from co-medications that induce or inhibit CYP enzymes and from comorbidities (e.g., HIV, hepatitis) be addressed. FDA also stated that many elements of its guidance on studies of devices intended to treat OUD will likely apply, and that the EMC guidance applies to the reader.
Since the Pre-Submission, CARI has completed the following design work. A Phase 1 (Requirements, Planning and Feasibility) design review was held on May 18, 2026 and approved with action items; the updated record (October 4, 2026) was routed for approval and its final approval is not yet in the data room. A first-in-human feasibility study (n=5, April 2025) and a retrospective 30-sample study against ARUP LC-MS/MS (August 2026) have been completed. The retrospective study reported EDDP R = 0.96, mean CV 3.9%, and optimized MTD R = 0.96, mean CV 2.4% (n=15). These are prototype results on plasma or serum, not fingerstick data. Bench work in 2026 resolved MTD/EDDP signal cross-talk and validated a hematocrit-correction model (R² = 0.9917). A custom cassette has been qualified for MTD and hematocrit; EDDP qualification on the integrated system is in progress.
Regulatory and Project Plan Report.Quality Management System:
CARI operates an electronic QMS (Ultralight by Greenlight Guru, migrated from Enzyme). Its Quality Policy (QPOL-001) is written to ISO 13485:2016 and FDA's Quality Management System Regulation (QMSR, 21 CFR Part 820), which took effect on February 2, 2026.³ The data room contains SOP-001 Document Control (Rev B), SOP-007 Supplier Management (Ver B), SOP-030 Design and Development (Rev B), the Phase 1 and Phase 2 design-review forms (SOP006-F-1/F-2), the Supplier Risk Assessment form (SOP007-F-2), the Risk Management Plan (RMP-001, per ISO 14971) and the organization chart (ORG-001). Product requirements (CID-001, PRD-001, PRD-002, PRD-003 draft) and the Design and Development Plan (DDP-001) are controlled in the eQMS.
The QMS is appropriate for a development-stage IVD company, but it is not yet complete for commercialization. Referenced procedures for design review (SOP-006) and risk management (SOP-008) are not in the data room, nor are procedures for CAPA, complaint handling, training, production and process controls, or management review. Document effective dates show only "See Export," so approval dates could not be verified from the copies provided. The Phase 1 review left six open action items for Phase 2:
[CALLOUT BOX] Control Kit Product Requirements Document (PRD-003)
[CALLOUT BOX] Human Factors and Usability Plan (not started)
[CALLOUT BOX] Design Trace Matrix
[CALLOUT BOX] Approved Software Plan, including review of IUL's reader software specification and risk file against FDA software submission requirements
[CALLOUT BOX] Design FMEA
[CALLOUT BOX] User FMEA / use-related risk analysis
The independent reviewer (Mike Hale, PhD) noted at that review that hematocrit effects must be addressed in the design, that the control kit would likely require a separate 510(k), and that FDA typically expects defined clinical cutoffs even where none are established in the literature.
Regulatory and Project Plan Report.Clinical Studies and IRB:
Clinical work is conducted under WCG IRB Protocol 004, "Assessing concentrations of methadone and its metabolites" (IRB tracking #20243811). The original approval (Board action March 20, 2025; Solaris Research Institute) expired on October 8, 2025. WCG granted continuing-review approval on September 22, 2026 for Synergy Research Centers (Lemon Grove, CA), valid through October 8, 2027. WCG IRB approved the amendment dated October 9, 2026 on October 20, 2026 (Certificates of Action for the protocol and for Study 1417787), with approval through October 8, 2027. It names Community Medical Services (Phoenix) as the site, with Dr. Robert Sherrick as investigator, and covers a clinical validation study of up to 500 participants, so later studies will not need further amendments. It describes only the quantitative measurement of methadone and EDDP and states that no clinical decisions or dose changes will be based on study results. Inclusion requires a methadone dose of at least 50 mg daily for seven days (80 mg preferred), and participants with anemia are excluded.
WCG designated the protocol "IDE exempt" in a phone call in October 2024, when the study used existing lateral flow assays rather than a CARI device. In the due diligence team's view, the exemption for diagnostic device studies under 21 CFR 812.2(c)(3) is likely to apply to the current fingerstick study, because sampling is non-significant-risk and results are not used for diagnosis without confirmation. However, the exemption is the sponsor's responsibility to determine. CARI should document its own written exemption rationale for the amended, device-based protocol rather than rely on the IRB's 2024 call.⁴ The data room does not contain a continuing-review record covering October 2025 to September 2026; this should be confirmed.
Regulatory and Project Plan Report.Project Timeline:
The project plan and timeline in the Regulatory Strategy, R&D Progress Summary, Board minutes and financial model were reviewed. The plan identifies the main steps to complete development, verify and validate the system, and obtain clearance and a CLIA waiver. Overall, the timeline is logical, but it is aggressive and leaves little contingency.
[TABLE]
Milestone | Company target | Due diligence team comment
30-patient pilot study (CMS) | December 2026 (date to be fixed by Nov 15) | IRB amendment approved October 20, 2026; results are expected about 4–6 weeks after the study, in early 2027.
Design freeze | End of Dec 2026 | At risk: reader software must be adapted for the custom cassette and hematocrit correction, and IUL cannot deliver final specifications until after the pilot. Development cost has not yet been quantified.
Second Pre-Submission | Q1 2027 | FDA written feedback took about 65 days on the first Pre-Submission; plan for about 70–75 days before the clinical validation study protocol is final. With pilot results in early 2027, a Q1 2027 submission is tight.
Validation lots; clinical validation study (~3 sites, ~150 patients) | 2027 (model: Jul–Sep 2027) | Requires Series A funding (targeted Aug 2027). The sample size must be statistically justified per FDA. Analytical studies (precision, interference, cross-reactivity, stability, lot-to-lot), software V&V, and EMC/electrical safety for the reader run in parallel.
510(k) submission and clearance (moderate complexity) | Submission 2027; clearance 2028 | Achievable if submitted by about Q4 2027. Typical total time to decision, including one additional-information request, is about 5–8 months.
CLIA waiver | 2028–2029 (Company target; previously later 2028) | The Company now targets 2028–2029 (Regulatory Strategy, October 26, 2026). Requires waiver studies with untrained operators in intended settings and a simplified workflow. The workflow described to FDA in 2025 (EDTA tube, 1:5 dilution, pipetting) would not qualify. 2029 is more realistic unless a Dual 510(k)/CLIA Waiver submission is used.
MMR De Novo (optional) | 2029 | Depends on clinical evidence of MMR validity; partly funded only if the $9.5M UG3/UH3 grant is awarded (decision March 2027).
[/TABLE]
Sources: Regulatory Strategy (Oct 2026); R&D Progress Summary (Oct 2026); Q3 2026 Board minutes; financial model; Q250159 correspondence.
This project has several significant challenges which may cause delays:
[CALLOUT BOX] The design is not frozen.
Design freeze slipped from June 30, 2026 to the end of December 2026 because solving hematocrit variation required a new invention and cassette. Until the reader software is complete and the integrated system (including EDDP) is qualified, parallel activities can only proceed at risk.
[CALLOUT BOX] Single reader supplier and software dependency.
The reader, its firmware and its risk file belong to IUL. The 510(k) will need adequate software documentation from IUL, and commercial supply depends on a supply agreement that is still in draft. The EDDP antibody is also single-sourced.
[CALLOUT BOX] New matrix and first quantitative claim.
No quantitative methadone or EDDP test on capillary blood has been cleared. Fingerstick collection is a known source of imprecision, and FDA requires capillary precision and matrix-equivalence data. To date, all accuracy data are from plasma or serum. Prospective fingerstick data will first come from the Q4 2026 pilot.
[CALLOUT BOX] Performance targets and clinical cutoffs.
CARI's internal target is CV ≤10%, while ±20% was discussed with FDA. FDA expects acceptance criteria tied to medical decision points, but there is no established therapeutic range for blood methadone. CARI will need to support its benefit–risk case with clinician input and literature.
[CALLOUT BOX] CLIA waiver drives the broad market.
Only a subset of OTPs operate moderate-complexity laboratories. The commercial plan beyond the largest operators depends on the waiver, which needs separate studies and a simple, robust workflow. Human factors work, which is essential for a waiver, has not started.
[CALLOUT BOX] Control kit pathway is undefined.
An internal reviewer expects a separate 510(k) for the control kit. This is not shown as a separate item in the regulatory timeline.
[CALLOUT BOX] Consistency of regulatory communications.
Some earlier materials characterized FDA's feedback more definitively than the meeting record, which describes the 510(k) approach as one that "seemed reasonable," and referred to MMR as a device feature. The Company has aligned its materials to the FDA record, but a submitted grant cover letter still contains MMR language and cannot be changed; MMR is a research aim for the optional De Novo. Future communications should track the FDA record exactly.
[CALLOUT BOX] Funding-dependent schedule.
The validation study and 510(k) submission depend on closing a $10M Series A in 2027 before FDA clearance, which the Board rates as its highest risk.
Regulatory and Project Plan Report.Conclusion/Summary:
### Regulatory
CARI Health, supported by experienced regulatory and product development consultants, has developed an appropriate regulatory strategy. The Pre-Submission produced substantive feedback, and CARI responded sensibly by removing MMR, defining the patient population and adopting a 510(k) under 21 CFR 862.3620 with a staged CLIA waiver and an optional De Novo. This has reduced regulatory risk compared with the De Novo CARI originally proposed. FDA feedback is advisory and non-binding, however, and FDA emphasized that this would be the first quantitative capillary-blood methadone/EDDP clearance. The key regulatory risks are the capillary-matrix performance data, acceptance criteria tied to clinically meaningful decision points, and an acceptable benefit–risk case.
### Project Plan
The project plan is well sequenced and is supported by a design-control framework, an eQMS and an experienced team. It is still aggressive: design freeze has already slipped, human factors and design risk analyses have not started, the reader software and supply depend on a single partner, and key studies depend on a Series A that is not yet raised. In the due diligence team's view, 510(k) clearance in 2028 is achievable but leaves no contingency, and a CLIA waiver is more likely in 2029 than in late 2028; the Company's documents now show 2028–2029. Considering the company's stage, the plan adequately identifies the activities needed to develop, verify, validate and submit the product. Investors should plan for some schedule slippage and the related funding need.
